text:
Today I'm launching Baby Whale 🐋

A local-first AI coworker that turns messy source material into finished work.

Not chat. Not suggestions. Files.

— Excel workbooks with live formulas, native charts, data bars
— PowerPoint decks with real layouts and speaker notes
— Word documents with covers, callouts, banded tables

The kind your boss can open without asking "why is this a CSV?"

How it works:

1. Drop your files into the chat (.xlsx, .csv, .docx)
2. Describe the outcome in plain words
3. Baby Whale reads the data, writes the code, builds the files, verifies them
4. Everything lands in deliverables/ on your disk

The pitch: most AI tools talk about work. Baby Whale does the work — with code, against the real formats. What you get stays editable.

Three things I refuse to compromise on:

🔒 Local-first, structurally. No Baby Whale cloud. No account. No telemetry. Your files never leave your machine — not because of a policy, but because there's no server that could take them.

🔑 Your key, your model. Bring your own API key — DeepSeek, OpenRouter, any compatible provider. Requests go from your machine straight to your provider.

🧩 Everything is a plugin. Seven knowledge-work skills ship built in — spreadsheets, decks, documents, data cleaning, research, PDFs, and a design system that keeps multi-file packs consistent. Don't need one? Switch it off and it's gone.

It even runs on a schedule: recurring tasks on a live task board, and missed runs get surfaced honestly instead of silently vanishing.

Getting started is one command:

npm i -g @haifai/bwhale

Then run anytime by typing: 
bwhale

First start fetches the runtime (once), opens the app in your browser, and you're working. Free and open source (MIT).

Baby Whale is built on DeepSeek Harness — an open-source agent harness where everything is a plugin. That architecture is the reason this works.

It's a public preview. It moves fast, it will break occasionally, and every change gets an honest changelog.

Try it. Break it. Tell me everything.

关善祥的“原教旨主义价值投资的条条框框和思想钢印”的教训：

1.“之前跟朋友说过一句话，跟严格止损、及时向市场认错的趋势交易相比，某种程度，价值投资的某些手法，才是真正的“赌博”。”

2.“芒格加杠杆价投阿里巴巴，最后临死前发现是在“赌博”。”

2021-2022，疫情期间，芒格都没法来中国、都没见过中国电商当时的生态，竟然敢一路下跌中加杠杆重仓抄底阿里巴巴。难道不是赌博吗？

2.“很多投资者都没接触、没用过过所投资公司的产品，没见过公司管理层、不认识任何一个公司员工，甚至都没去过美国，甚至美国签证都被拒（比如我），投资美股信息层面天然具备劣势。如果盲目按照机构声称的 “原教旨主义价值投资的条条框框和思想钢印”来操作，那不是笑话吗？"

在这种情况下，如果信誓旦旦地说能看懂美股里的某个行业或某个企业的终局、五年、十年后的未来，难道不是赌博吗？

3.胡猛：我经常跟很多基金经理开玩笑说：“一个上市公司的CEO都不知道自己的企业明年的利润会怎么样。凭什么你一个外部投资者，信誓旦旦地认为这公司明年会怎么样，十年后会怎么样？”

马化腾、比尔盖茨当初刚上市时如果能看懂自己企业五年后、十年后的未来，就不会一路减仓了。

又一个被证伪的case：

刚看到一个新闻，雪球有个A 股投资大V叫U兄（关善祥）去世，40岁。

他2020年初还发了私募基金，三年以来亏损-60%以上。

有点震惊。

因为之前在雪球看过他的文章，后来还买过他写的一本书，讲价值投资的，觉得还可以，属于值得看一遍，但不值得看三遍的那种。

印象很深的是后来他讲投资是个长期事业，要活到120岁，所以非常注重饮食、锻炼、睡眠、空气和水的质量。

所以9月28日下午3点基金发公告说去世（图1），大概率不是什么疾病或猝死，而是主动自杀。

自杀原因：
他的私募全仓在融创、万科、保利、平安，而且之前在融创连续下跌中，觉得越跌越便宜，所以不断调仓抄底加大仓位。（图3、4）。

昨天早上恒大停牌、许家印被抓，应该是压垮他的最后一根稻草，内心对地产股的幻想和希望破灭。

发私募管理别人的钱，很多都是线下跟他见面深入交流的粉丝，脸皮太薄，所以选择自杀。

看他在雪球上写的，自视一个把（A股）价值投资者视作生命的人，当自己深信不疑、引以为豪、且大肆宣传的投资理念被证伪时，承受不了这种幻灭感和挫败感。

对于充满局限性和有限条件的个人美股投资者而言，“基本面驱动的纪律型成长股趋势交易”体系，之所以比“原教旨主义价值投资的条条框框和思想钢印”体系大概率更容易上手、更适用。

我觉得原因有如下几个：

1.美股市场本身更阳谋、更强势、风格更逐强，突破、破位有效的概率比大A市场、web3市场更高。（所以提醒你：别把标准泳姿用于泥坑或粪坑池子）。

2.很多投资者都没接触、没用过过所投资公司的产品，没见过公司管理层、不认识任何一个公司员工，甚至都没去过美国，甚至美国签证都被拒（比如我），投资美股信息层面天然具备劣势。如果盲目按照机构声称的
“原教旨主义价值投资的条条框框和思想钢印”来操作，那不是笑话吗？

3.而且很多机构言必称这些条条框框和思想钢印，他们的实际目的是融资、给投资人洗脑，实际投资做的很差。如胡猛所说：“你这是融资的语言，而不是投资的语言。”

推荐看看欧奈尔、Mark Minervini、吴伟志的书，对冲下这些条条框框和思想钢印的毒。

text:
Since the beginning of summer, we've all noticed how liquidity on Polymarket gradually started to decline, and at this point, the drop has reached significant proportions.

While previously you could boost liquidity through sponsored rewards, now, even after deploying a significant amount of capital and landing in the top 5 markets by yield, nobody is in any rush to farm rewards. Bots and airdrop farmers went offline back in the summer, and the massive influx of new markets is essentially useless without the necessary liquidity.

Now, to get your orders filled, you sometimes have to wait for weeks, and even then, in most cases you never get the share volume you need.

It's all snowballing: CLOB issues, lack of liquidity, the exodus of bots and farmers - it's very bad, and the team's lack of sound communication and a clear roadmap only exacerbates the situation.

In all my time trading on Polymarket, I've never complained and always tried to maintain an optimistic attitude, but now, after so long, my outlook on the situation is beginning to turn pessimistic.

text:
MY $Buttcoin THESIS 🍑

I’ve held $Buttcoin for 8 months without selling. It’s one of the very few small-cap memes I can hold and still sleep peacefully at night.
Why? Because while the token launched in early 2026, Buttcoin’s lore goes all the way back to 2011, two years before DOGE even existed.

It started as a parody of Bitcoin. 15 years later, the joke came full circle and became an on-chain asset, launched by the original Buttcoin creator from 2011.
Think about how rare that is.

Most memecoins launch first and desperately try to build lore afterward, only to pump and dump within a week or a month.
Buttcoin survived 15 YEARS before it even became a coin.

You can copy the ticker.
You can copy the meme.
You can manufacture a narrative.
But you can’t manufacture 15 years of history.

That’s why I don’t see $Buttcoin as another typical pump-and-dump that appears, pumps, and disappears.
I see it as a potential multicycle meme.

My conviction grew even stronger when UHNWI Matt Beall accumulated roughly 9% of the supply and locked his coins. Nobody knows when he’ll eventually sell, but that level of commitment is hard to ignore.

But the core of my thesis is simple:
The market still hasn’t fully priced what Buttcoin is.
My comfort holding $Buttcoin is comparable to established multicycle memes like DOGE, SHIB and PEPE.
The difference?
They’ve already had their major price discovery. Buttcoin hasn’t.

I don’t see 8 figures as the destination. I see it as the beginning of price discovery. In a true bull market, my thesis is that $Buttcoin can eventually reach a 9-figure valuation once the market starts to realize what Buttcoin actually is and prices it accordingly.

And then there’s the prophecy that has existed since the beginning:
10,000 $Buttcoin = 1 BITCOIN.
What started as absurd internet humor in 2011 is finally an on-chain asset 15 years later.

Maybe the prophecy was just a joke.
Or maybe the joke has been waiting 15 years for the market to catch up.

In a market filled with thousands of manufactured narratives and tokens that disappear as quickly as they arrive, I believe $Buttcoin is like a diamond hidden among billions of grains of sand.

Sand is everywhere.

Diamonds aren’t. 💎🍑

text:
This intern 6x'd her company's website traffic with an AI content machine called BlogEO. 

The big f*cking problem
- Blog had almost no real measurement
- Insights lived in ~5 places (GSC, Semrush, PostHog, Sanity, prior run snapshots) so nobody joined the data
- ~70% of traffic came from 14 posts; ~50% from just 5
- Top SEO posts were often invisible to LLMs (AEO gap)

Step 1: Run the AI audit
- Pulls those five sources into one view
- Content hygiene scan first: broken links, positioning drift, deprecated products
- Broken-link fixes use @browserbase's fetch API to find the right replacement
- Broken links + missing SEO fields can auto-publish (no human gate)
- Scores every post into a ranking / opportunity queue
- Flags the top ~15 for deeper fact-check + SEO verification
- Drafts surgical edits (small, intentional) and stores each suggestion
- Edits stay small on purpose. Most posts were handwritten; don’t paste AI voice over human voice
- High-leverage changes: SEO title, meta description, swap a link
- 28-day cooldown after changes so GSC has time to catch up (no thrashing the same post)

Step 1b: Score post opportunities
• Unit of opportunity = clicks
• Click recovery: if clicks fell hard vs the last ~28 days, that lost volume is opportunity. Real click loss beats any estimate and jumps the queue.
• CTR gap: compare your CTR at a given position to what page-one / peers get at that same spot. Gap × impressions ≈ clicks you’re leaving on the table. (Alex’s example: position 9 averages ~5% CTR; you’re at 1% → the 4-pt delta is the opportunity.)
• Rank upside: if you’re on page 2/3, estimate clicks if you moved to page 1 / to the average for that better position. (Her example: post at 9.4 with a pink-dot underperform → ~7,400 click opportunity if it hit the average for that position.)
• Queue, then spend: every post gets a cheap score; only the top ~15 get the expensive fact-check / deep SEO pass (token control). Near-invisible / irrelevant queries don’t score high on purpose.

Step 3: Avoid AI slop
- New posts aren’t a firehose ideas surface as drafts, ~once a week
- Ignore / skip is a first-class option if the query isn’t worth owning
- Quality gate before anything ships
- Slack card shows who approved and who published — accountability stays with a person
- Human pride > “we shipped another AI blog”

 Step 4: Run the full blog machine
- Weekly cadence in Slack: Monday = content generation, Tuesday = audit (plus on-demand “audit this page now”)
- Agent (BB) has skills: audit, strategy, writing, generate...always drafts suggestions first
- Agent has no write path to live content until a human clicks
- Slack cards: Approve / Edit / Skip / Discard → only then does it hit the CMS
- Approved edits + outcomes land in internal DBs (including what never shipped)
- Near-miss queries (show up in search, no targeted page) feed the generator side

The results
Search impressions: +5.8x
Page-one queries: +9.8x
Avg blog position: page 2 → page 1

Massive shoutout to @harsehaj for the amazing internship project & masterclass in AI-powered AEO/SEO!

text:
Elon would tell you to find the bottleneck and attack it relentlessly.

What @ZachBDell learned from working with people who worked closely with Elon:

“I've learned a lot of this from Antonio Gracias who's on my board and has worked very closely with Elon for decades. 

Every conversation with Antonio was the same: 

"Hey Antonio how's it going?

"Zach what's your constraint? What's the constraint of the business?

And I would just answer the question and that's all we would talk about. 

What's the constraint? 
What's the constraint? 
What's the constraint?

Let's just focus all of our time and energy on that.

It forces you to focus on the uncomfortable thing. 

We need to be constantly asking what is constraining us towards our mission? Let's just focus on that. 

It's incredibly clarifying and uncomfortable. 

The natural tendency is to talk about all the different things that are going on and all the different opportunities available to you.

And the hard thing is to focus on the most important thing, the constraint in-between you and your goal. 

What constraints can we relieve? That’s really the only thing that matters and all the other stuff is just noise.”

text:
我基于 @BNBCHAIN  ，实现了历史上第一次在L1主网上跑Linux。这是第一个每条指令都由 L1 主网交易执行、全部状态都存在 L1 上的 Linux。
此前这个领域公认的先行者是 Cartesi：它的 RISC-V 虚拟机能启动完整的 Linux，但 Linux 是在链下节点上跑的，以太坊 L1 只负责结算，只有当参与者对结果有争议时，才把争议的那一步拿到链上重算。正常情况下，L1 从头到尾没有执行过一条 Linux 指令。它是 L2 框架，靠欺诈证明和至少一个诚实的挑战者。
而TapeOut做的是真正的，Linux 的每一条指令都在 BNBChain 主网的交易里由验证者算出来，并且拥有32 个寄存器、全部 CSR以及16 MB 内存的每一页都在BNBChain主网上，没有任何链下执行。也就是说Cartesi 上让 L1 能验证 Linux，我们让BNBChain 真实的链上运行完整的 Linux。
它是由TapeOut 的电路+容器组成，第一次组成了一台完整的链上计算机。一片电路（#4246）开通了容器，容器成了这台机器的主人，谁持有这片电路的 NFT，谁就是它的管理员。CPU 是一个 RISC-V 元件，内存是 16 MB、按 1 KB 分页的 16,384 个页合约，写时复制。主板合约用交易跑指令，把改过的内存页写回链上，把串口输出发成事件。
装的是 kernelorg 主线 Linux 6.5.12，它从复位向量 0x80000000 上电，在主网上安拍跑完整个内核启动，直到 root 登录：一共44,988 拍，9,000 余笔交易（花了我好多bnb啊，有点肉疼，另外我还找bnbchain的小伙伴申请了10个tBNB做的测试网测试，感谢 @0xSandy1913 帮助协调测试网的tBNB）。
另外呢，任何人都可以用它。打开 https://t.co/SpeMEejeFq，像用真实终端一样直接敲命令：uname -a 会告诉你这是 riscv32 上的 Linux 6.5.12；factor 1000000007 在链上做一次质因数分解；echo 写一个文件，这个文件就住在主网上某一页合约的字节码里，你能在 BscScan 上看见它，谁使用谁自己付 gas（我可支付不起这么多人测试，哈哈）。

这件事说明： @BNBCHAIN  不只是一个公共账本，它可以基于TapeOut承载可验证的生产工具，一台计算机是所有生产工具的底座。

text:
$ZCSH $ZEC They Will Not Ask You. They Will Say the Food Was Good.

​If you manage other people’s money and hold Bitcoin in the book, 2026 is not necessarily the year clients debate privacy coins with you. It is the year some of them answer the question without you and leave.

​The review will go fine. They will shake your hand. Months later, the CRM will record the departure as “consolidation.”

​It is the classic restaurant problem:
“How was everything?”
“Good.”

And then they never come back.

​This cuts hardest in a family office, where a handful of consequential relationships are anchored entirely to the story of the manager. There is no nine-member investment committee to absorb a blind spot; the principal is the committee.

​When you put them into Bitcoin early, it was still socially embarrassing to the room and courageous to the client. In doing so, you trained them to recognize a specific lifecycle:

First it looks like a fringe experiment.
Custody is messy; compliance hates it.
Then infrastructure arrives, a wrapper appears, and the room changes its mind.

​Now Zcash is running that exact playbook: an ETF wrapper, institutional volume, and a supply-capped design arriving just as transparent ledgers become a surveillance liability for private wealth.

​Wealthy families aren’t running factor models; they are hearing a rhyme. And the rhyme is most dangerous if you were the person who taught them how to listen.

​They will not send an email with the subject line Why Don't We Own ZEC?

They won't ask for a seminar on Orchard pools or AML compliance. 

The client asks something much more personal:
​You were the person willing to sit in the embarrassment on purpose. If that instinct survived success, wouldn't you at least have had a line on this?

​A fiduciary can have excellent reasons to pass—shielded-pool verification friction, liquidity thresholds, or strict mandate limits. But silence is deadly. Buying ZEC late is not courage, but pretending the category doesn't exist makes you look house-trained.

​The relationship risk is not failing to buy ZEC at $50. The danger is appearing intellectually incurious when another cypherpunk monetary asset crosses into mainstream financial infrastructure.

​You do not have to own ZEC. You have to demonstrate that you made the observation.

​A one-page note sent before the client asks—stating that privacy money is an investable category, why you passed, and the conditions under which you'd revisit it—tells them the radar still works. Silence tells them you were a pioneer until pioneering became a product category, and then you became an indexer.

​There are only three clean positions:

​Privacy is outside the mandate, and here is why Bitcoin's transparent graph remains acceptable.

​Privacy is now in the mandate, so here is a sized satellite allocation and our kill criteria.

​We missed an emerging asset class; here is what failed in our process and what changes.

​Otherwise, every time you market that you got them into Bitcoin early, you invite the only question that matters:

​Early on what now?

text:
The hottest category in tech right now is AI assistants.

The question is; who is going to win?

Instinct raised at $2.5BN. Has Benchmark and Index behind them.

Grok Bot is ripping with Elon and has the distribution machine of X.

And then there is Town, one of the only ones that’s actually making real money from real businesses.

Don’t write Zuck off. This will be his next play and integrated into every WhatsApp user’s product.

I sat down with Town Founder, @jgreze to understand WTF is going on, who wins and who loses?

Condensed my notes below!

1. We Have Passed the Point Where Humans Look at Lines of Code

Software engineering has crossed a threshold where machines increasingly write and ship code into production under model-based guardrails. Outside critical security controls, humans will spend far less time reviewing raw code. The future belongs to systems that manage autonomous AI agents writing software, running tests, and validating their own work.

2. You Can Build at the Speed of Machines, but You Can Only Learn at the Speed of Humans

AI development tools allow competitors to clone features in weeks, erasing traditional software head starts. But deep user feedback cannot be automated. While machines accelerate execution, true competitive advantage comes from maximizing human learning cycles and understanding customers faster than anyone else.

3. Why None of the AI Assistants Have True Product-Market Fit Today

Despite immense market hype, no current AI assistant has achieved deep product-market fit with mainstream users. Most products still cater primarily to power users rather than everyday workers. Before worrying about moats, founders need to create frictionless experiences that resonate with the mass market.

4. Network Effects at the Agent Level Will Separate AI Winners

Sustainable moats in AI assistants will come from multi-user network effects at the agent level, not single-player productivity. When autonomous assistants collaborate across teams to resolve queries and execute work, switching becomes increasingly difficult. Multiplayer workflows create organizational lock-in that personal assistants cannot replicate.

5. How Much of the Workload Stays at the Frontier Versus Open Weight?

AI application margins depend heavily on how much work requires expensive frontier models versus cheaper open weights. Complex reasoning may still demand frontier intelligence, while routine tasks like scheduling and email tagging continue moving down the cost curve. Shifting 80% of workloads to open weights over time could create far more sustainable economics.

6. My R&D Is Just Spent Getting Product Parity With the Giants

Competing with giants like OpenAI requires massive investment simply to maintain feature parity. Startups cannot rely on unique distribution if their underlying harness falls behind on core capabilities. AI assistants must invest heavily to match the execution speed and product depth of frontier teams.

7. Why Instinct Is Not a Competitor to Town

Consumer assistants like Instinct focus on rapid acquisition through subsidized personal tools, while enterprise platforms build monetizable team workflows. Although their technical harnesses may overlap, their target ICPs and business models diverge sharply. Enterprise agents monetize by embedding collaboration directly into daily operations.

Going fully onchain changes the oracle model completely.

Instead of asking projects to pay upfront for a price feed and maintain dedicated infrastructure, Mimir distributes that cost across actual usage. Any project can plug in with almost no friction, while the extra cost for users stays tiny.

But this is where it gets interesting: every new feed becomes a piece of infrastructure owned by its creator. Other feeds can build on it, applications can use it, and that activity generates fees back to the people building the oracle.

The network pays for the infrastructure as it uses it, and users become its builders.

This is Oracle 3.0.

RH 核心还是龙头价格，龙头价格取决于拥有影响力的车头和项目方的动作。 @theunipcs 为此专门发了长文，Long 也在积极地放出信号，所以我觉得情绪还会回来的。重点会看 Long eco，另外值得关注的就是各种 DeFi ponzi。我觉得套娃的 Launchpad 不具备持续性。

在我的角度来看，Solana 持续炒作的可能性比较低，一是 Solana 上基础设施很完备，类似 RH 基础设施 Ponzi 模式很难炒作起来；二是该玩的 meme 都已经在 RH 炒过了，纯复制粘贴我觉得没啥太大的意思。所以现在 Solana 上炒作的其实不是 RWA，而是 meme/ZEC、HYPE、TAO 的 pair。

BSC 现在的主线就是台子竞争，新台子就是 BREW、AST 这些。不过我觉得现在反复琢磨这些台子意义不大，说到底还是需要情绪，龙头跌跌不休的话，情绪起不来。

说到底，主线还会是 RH，因为它够原生，够野性，Web2 的影响力也在持续引导情绪，是一个非常完美的主战场。而 BSC 背景好，所以也要分一部分精力去看。而 Solana，我觉得还是一个支线试炼。

text:
今天一整天都在开发Obsidian插件，几个经验分享：

1. 在GPT-6 Astra 帮助下，开发和上架难度远比想像的低。

2. 插件要传 Github，官方有自动扫描工具检查代码，main.js 不能超过5m，提示影响插件同步。

扫描通过后，会出现在官网社区。但 Obsidian 内置社区插件商店不会立即显示，有审核延迟。

插件不允许上传图片Logo，只能管理后台选 SVG icon加背景色。

3. 插件最好设计成移动端友好，这样手机Obsidian也能用。

4. 建议弄一个新 Github仓库，如果你fork一个基础代码改造，上架时会要求证明上游同意你发布。

最后，产品要充分利用Obsidian 已有能力和组件。

比如插件需要用户设文件夹，浏览选择比让用户手输入靠谱和简单。

text:
ok, read this to understand SHROOM

on RH RWAs are all a lil volatile, and are being paired with memes that are super volatile, while all the pools for them have high fees

its only natural and expected for a new medium of exchange to develop to pair with ALL the RWAs to eat up all the fees and get routed through regularly

I think people don't understand this, because they're likely thinking 'but we have stablecoins you cretin'

The thing, if the medium of exchange is volatile, there will be frequent arbitrage opportunities against the RWAs for MMs and aggregators to inevitably route through to make a few bps. 

The bigger the depth of liquidity is on those arb opportunities, the more money those pools will make for the new volatile medium of exchange token/protocol

the game is to grow liquidity enough in pairs with that new MOE that it then begets more volume, that then begets more fees, that then creates more liquidity through fees being used to shure up the pools (and to give back to holders via distributions of RWAs/buybacks).

it's a flywheel (shoot me, but it is)

SHROOM is the category leader. 

It has nothing special about it in terms of tech moat, other than it has that je ne sais quoi to become the breakout token for this purpose, and a cracked thoughtful dev team who are tweaking things to max out the fee capture/liquidity expansion over time. 

buying SHROOM is a bet on it being the new robinhood 'liquidity layer' token, and it having a pareto distribution (capture 80% of the market whilst there's a longtail of smaller tokens trying the same thing) by being the first mover to reach escape velocity.

If the RWA/meme or RWA/volatile-token trading volume continues on RH (seems likely to me), SHROOM could become very, very, very big.

text:
The case for *total* Linux victory (desktop, mobile, server, iot, robots, embedded…):

1) Most agent-programmable
People will want fully personalized computing experiences. macOS makes it hard to even ship a tiny app to your menubar.

2) Open source training data
Blender beats all its competitors because it's optimal in the most important dimension: agents can train on it and use it efficiently. OSS wins.

3) Design being democratized
macOS has historically had a 'monopoly' on beautiful OS design. The global design community is now huge, they're motivated, they have tokens.

4) Computing moving to cloud sandboxes
More and more of our personal and professional computing experiences will come from agents that orchestrate work in the cloud, using sandboxes. Those sandboxes will be Linux. Bonus: seamless continuum between local & remote

5) Security
Every piece of software is now at major risk, Linux included. But Linux has the collective investment of everyone on the planet throwing tokens at it.

text:
Long-horizon agents are one of the most interesting ways to get genuinely novel work out of models, but the failure surface is huge. A run can call the wrong tool, follow a bad plan for twenty steps, lose track of its state, or confidently decide it has finished when it hasn’t.

After running a bunch of longer experiments, the broader pattern I keep coming back to is the jaggedness of model capability, which I first saw @karpathy mention. A model can look much stronger in aggregate and still fail on a task that a smaller, cheaper model handles cleanly.

Some of that likely comes from differences in training data, post-training objectives, reasoning behavior, and tool-use priors. Long-horizon tasks are diverse enough that no single model covers the entire failure surface.

So I built a simple supervisor to test the most naive implication: run one model, evaluate its work with an external verifier, and, if it fails, restart cleanly with a model that has a different capability profile.

Across 18 sealed tasks, the best single model completed 7/18. The four-model portfolio completed 12/18 at a slightly lower replayed model cost, pushing the observed completion-cost Pareto frontier outward.

It’s still an early result, but it suggests that reliability for long-running agents may come less from finding one universally “best” model and more from composing several imperfect, complementary ones.

Results below:

author: alexisohanian
quoted_text:
A friend who just got their labs back asked me how to actually think about ApoB vs LDL vs Lp(a).

The analogy that's helped me most: think of your arteries as a highway (insert all oversimplification caveats).
- LDL-C measures the total cargo on the road: how much cholesterol is being carried.
- ApoB counts the cars: every particle that can cause plaque carries exactly one ApoB, so it's literally a particle count.
- Lp(a) counts the cars towing trailers: mostly set by your genes. 

Why this matters: heart disease starts when a particle gets stuck in the artery wall. So your risk depends more on how many particles are on the road than on how much cholesterol they're carrying. Two people can both have an LDL of 130 while one has 50% more particles (image attached). And when the two numbers differ, risk follows the particle count (ApoB).

In 389,529 UK Biobank adults followed for ~11 years, ApoB was the only lipid number still linked to heart attacks after accounting for the others. LDL added essentially nothing beyond it.

Lp(a) is the one most people haven't heard of. It's an LDL particle with a sticky tail attached (the trailer), and particle for particle it's about 6.6x more likely to cause plaque than regular LDL. About 1 in 5 people have high Lp(a). It's ~90% genetic, and diet and exercise barely move it. As I wrote Friday, drugs can move it, but that hasn't yet been proven to change outcomes (it's early).

The practical takeaway: ask your doctor to add ApoB to your next panel (it's cheap), and check Lp(a) at least once in your life.

A few call outs: the analogy ignores particle size, time in circulation, and the biology of the artery wall, and the 50% example is illustrative (insert all caveats).

Count the cars (ApoB), not just the cargo (LDL-C).

text:
Anthropic 最值钱的产品部门只有 20 个人。

Business Insider 今天扒出了 Anthropic 内部的 Labs。

这是联合创始人 Ben Mann 2024 年拉起来的一支小队，常驻成员只有大约 20 人。玩法很简单，一个想法先做，两周之后过一次 review，能跑就继续，跑不通直接杀掉或者并进别的项目，人马上去做下一件事。

他们内部统计的成功率只有 20% 到 30%。

Claude Code 是这里做出来的，MCP 是这里做出来的，今年的 Claude Design 也是。项目一旦验证成立、团队长到大约 4 个人以上，就从 Labs 里毕业，出去单独成立团队。于是 Labs 永远保持二十来个人，继续往下赌。

Claude Code 的故事最典型。2024 年底，Labs 提前从内部研究团队知道，新模型在 agentic coding 上已经开始出现明显能力，于是 Ben Mann 把 Boris Cherny 拉来试。Cherny 原本想做代码分析工具，Mann 觉得野心太小，让他重新想。几个月后，Claude Code 出来了。

这可能也是 AI 公司开始出现的一种很有意思的组织形态。

以前做产品，失败一次很贵，所以公司喜欢做调研、开会、排 roadmap，尽量把一个项目论证清楚再动手。

模型把 prototype 的成本压下来以后，逻辑开始反过来了。二十个人可以不停开新坑，允许八成想法死掉，只要剩下两成里偶尔长出一个 Claude Code。

quoted_text:
Codex usage dropping unusually fast, even after you stop working?

I put together a prompt to investigate, apply supported local fixes where possible, and generate a sanitized report.

Run it in your affected client, review the report, then DM it to me so I can compare findings.

Community diagnostic, not an official OpenAI tool or a guaranteed fix. The prompt authorizes reversible local changes.

Copy everything between START PROMPT and END PROMPT.

──── START PROMPT ────

CODEX USAGE CHECK v1.0

Investigate and actively fix avoidable Codex usage consumption in my environment. Include unexpected allowance changes after apparent inactivity.

Do not stop at an audit or recommendations. Apply supported, reversible fixes when the evidence identifies a local cause, then verify them.

Keep this investigation efficient: inspect relevant configuration and up to five recent affected tasks. Do not launch subagents, run expensive benchmarks or scan my entire session archive.

1. ESTABLISH THE ENVIRONMENT

Identify my OS, client names and exact versions. Include Codex desktop, CLI, IDE extensions or third-party clients such as Pi and T3 Code where present.

Determine authentication type and whether usage draws from a ChatGPT subscription allowance or separately billed API access. Never expose credentials.

Check the effective model, reasoning effort, Standard/Fast speed and task/project overrides. Do not assume the standalone CLI and desktop app share the same runtime or settings.

Record the subscription tier and usage window where verifiable. Distinguish allowance percentages, purchased credits and API billing.

2. INVESTIGATE THE CAUSE

Separate expensive active tasks from allowance updates observed after work stops.

Inspect:
- Relevant global/project instructions, injected memories, skills and tool context.
- Duplication, unnecessary context loading, broad searches and repeated checks.
- Context-window or compaction overrides and input-cache reuse.
- Active tasks, agents, hooks, automations, queues and background services.
- Duplicate workers, excessive retries, prompt replay and requests continuing after cancellation.
- Other clients or devices sharing the account, where observable.

Correlate task completion/cancellation, request timestamps, response identifiers and usage snapshots. Distinguish when requests happened from when usage became visible.

An open connection or running process alone is not evidence of model consumption. Missing telemetry is not zero usage. Do not double-count cumulative counters, cached input or reasoning tokens. Local token totals are not billed credits.

Use current official documentation and the installed client’s supported configuration. Treat delayed reporting and accounting defects as hypotheses unless established.

3. APPLY REVERSIBLE FIXES

You are authorized to:
- Switch Fast speed to Standard where enabled.
- Correct demonstrably invalid or obsolete usage-related configuration.
- Consolidate duplicated instructions while preserving their meaning.
- Narrow unnecessary searches, retries and repeated verification.
- Repair demonstrated duplicate scheduling, replay or cancellation problems.
- Pause clearly obsolete or unintended duplicate automations and stop clearly orphaned work after preserving resumable state.

Back up affected files before editing. Preserve my selected model and reasoning effort, legitimate ongoing work, necessary tests, security controls, preferences, credentials, memories, history and projects.

Do not purge caches or history as a presumed credit-saving trick. Do not enable experimental features solely on unsupported savings claims. Do not purchase credits, consume resets or change subscriptions.

Validate changes and check effective behavior. Revert changes that fail validation. Finish all independent work before explaining any required restart, new task or user decision.

4. VERIFY POST-INACTIVITY CONSUMPTION

If continued consumption after stopping is part of the symptom, prepare a lightweight local observation lasting at least 75 minutes.

Use existing logs and supported read-only usage telemetry where available. The observation must make no model calls or repeatedly wake an AI agent.

Exclude this audit’s own activity. Start only when a genuine idle interval can be established. Otherwise provide the exact launch command and explain what must finish first.

Record the observation’s coverage and limitations. Do not claim verified inactivity across unobserved devices or clients.

5. CREATE A SHAREABLE REPORT

Save codex-usage-report.md and provide its location plus a concise, copyable DM summary.

Include:

A. SUMMARY
Prompt version: CODEX USAGE CHECK v1.0.
Report identifier unrelated to account identity.
UTC date.
Outcome: FIXED / PARTIALLY FIXED / NO LOCAL CAUSE FOUND / INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE.
Reported symptom, onset and whether reproduced.

B. ENVIRONMENT
OS, clients, versions, authentication type, subscription tier, effective model, reasoning effort, speed and relevant context overrides.
Identify unknown values and unobserved clients.

C. EVIDENCE
A compact timeline of model activity and allowance observations.
Identify the usage window, whether percentages mean used or remaining, reset times, sources and measurement coverage.

D. FIXES
For each finding: evidence, confidence, exact change, validation result and rollback method.
Confidence: CONFIRMED / SUSPECTED / UNKNOWN.

E. IDLE OBSERVATION
Status: COMPLETED / RUNNING / NOT RUN.
Actual duration, observed clients, new requests, allowance change and possible interference.
Mark unfinished reports PRELIMINARY. Have the local sampler save its results without further model calls.

F. CONCLUSION
Separate verified facts from hypotheses, and expected savings from measured savings.
State unresolved issues and the evidence needed to investigate them. Do not claim a billing problem is fixed without evidence.

6. SANITIZE BEFORE SHARING

Check the report for credentials, cookies, authorization headers, account identifiers, emails, private prompts, source code, task titles, repository names, IP addresses and personal filesystem paths. Remove them.

Use consistent pseudonyms where identifiers are needed to correlate events. Keep original evidence locally for possible support follow-up.

Do not include raw transcripts or full configuration dumps. Do not send anything externally yourself.

text:
"AI solved problem XYZ open for N number of years" is a bad metric for measuring effectiveness of AI in solving frontier science problems.

The issue here being a problem open for 30 years might not mean that humanity collectively has dedicated 30 years of serious intellectual effort in trying to solve. It might have remained open because it is truly difficult but it may equally remain open because it is obscure, low-value or simply attracted low attention.

What ideally should be measured is total competent search expended on a problem, and that should be a better proxy for difficulty of a problem. 

Measuring difficulty of a problem requires measuring total attempted search in solving the problem, which requires metering system to be able to observe failed attempts, which requires incentivizing the disclosure of outcomes from failed attempts. Lack of a robust metering system in existing scientific publication means we have to use "open for N numbers of years" as a bad proxy for problem difficulty.

Surprisingly, if any metering system for "proof of verified effort" for scientific research were to exist, it seems to have close analogy with proof-of-work (PoW) from Bitcoin. 

First, such a system would need a difficulty adjustment mechanism to programmatically calibrate whether any given problem is anymore frontier or not based on recent submissions. If agents begin solving a benchmark routinely, the acceptance threshold can be strengthened: prove a stronger result, or satisfy a more demanding verifier. This can be reflected using reward adjustment. Problems receiving excessive compute relative to their scientific value might receive lower marginal incentives, while valuable but under-explored problems could receive larger ones. 

Second, incentivizing negative effort is akin to how mining pools work in Bitcoin. Imagine a conjecture P. Suppose agent A spends 1 million tokens solving an intermediate lemma, agent B spends 3 million tokens to discover that an entire family of approaches don't work, agent C spends 500k tokens to solve the conjecture. Both agent A and B should get a share of the total rewards, instead of just agent C as it happens in existing research system. This is similar in spirit to pool mining in Bitcoin: https://t.co/KmTZf7KXIE

Third, if most grunt work can be better be done by AI and humans operate at a more high abstract level (while manually steering and interacting their agents), then a cumulative sum of all receipts containing input tokens, output tokens, model number, CoT, tool calls, etc., might be a much better proxy for difficulty of the problem. It is a fascinating to note that pre-AI, it was not even possible to tally that from a human researcher doing the grunt work.

1) Use @ambire as your main wallet; it handles simulation, complex tx, and is designed to work well with @safe 
2) Deploy a Safe now. I don't care if it's a 1/1 linked to your hot wallet for now; it's fine. It's already better this way, and with Ambire, using it is seamless. 

YOU DO NOT HAVE TO USE THE SAFE UI; Ambire will do it all for you.

3a) Generate a real seed; use pen and paper. You'll get the fancy steel stuff later if you want. 

3b) Too lazy for the seed stuff? ok, use a "hotwallet" for your signer generated with a passkeys with an good password manager, you have a Mac? The Passwords app is fine; you're a Revolut client? NordPass is included; you ready to spend a bit? 1Password has a great API, and you'll love it once you're AI-pilled.

5) The signer wallet must hold no funds, doesn't hold gas, doesn't do any txs; it's the key to unlock the door of your safe; it signs, and that's it. You'll learn later that proposing (creating tx), signing, and executing tx are 3 different jobs that don't need to be done by the same wallets.

Step 2 is buying a hardware wallet and rotating the safe signer with it for much safer holding

Once you're there, you can start considering a 1/2 with a second hw or with an old phone you have in your drawer that you've factory reset and will use only for that. You keep it out of easy reach; it's your insurance if something bad happens to your main signer.

Then maybe a 2/3 and the nerdy stuff; you can always do "better," but the foundation of all that is getting your first safe deployed and climbing from there.

Do it now; it's not hard, it's worth it.

Today is a special day for me.

I've made $3M with my 36 startups.

Solo.
85% margin.
Bootstrapped.

It took 10 years, and I loved every second of it.

After failing as an entrepreneur for 5 years, I got a job in 2021.

That's when I discovered @levelsio's journey and decided to try again.

"If he can do it, maybe I can too?"

So I started building tiny startups and writing about it.

2021 and 2022 were quiet, but I was having fun.

Everything changed in 2023 when I launched ShipFast and made my first million.

Building something people finally paid for and enjoyed made me so happy.

My first 5 years of failures taught me not to get emotionally attached to a project, because everything goes to 0 eventually.

So I just kept shipping.

It's 2026, and I've launched 36 startups.

50% never made money.
Only 11% made decent money.

Back in 2016, when I started, I believed I would make it.

If I had known it would take 7 years of failure, I probably would never have started.

That's why I'm stupidly optimistic.

I don't think in years. I don't dream big.

I think in weeks. I build tiny projects fast. And I quit even faster.

That's how I wake up happy, enjoy the journey, and eventually build life-changing projects.

If you've been following the journey, thank you. You've given my posts a sense of purpose, which has kept me going, and I'm very grateful for this. ❤️

text:
Many of you have followed me here for years. You know the subjects I work on, the sources I care about, and the degree to which I obsess over language, texts, manuscripts, history, and the traditions surrounding them.

So when I say I think what I have been building may be significant, I hope you know I do not say that casually.

For roughly the past six months, I have been working intensely on a project that I have largely kept private. It sits at the intersection of Tora study, language, textual scholarship, technology, and AI.

Until now, I have spent most of that time building the foundation myself.

A few weeks ago, a good friend and teacher pushed me to present a small part of it at the Sephardic Rabbinic Conference. I had only a short amount of time to demonstrate what I had built and explain where I thought it could go. The reaction in the room convinced me that it was time to begin thinking much more seriously about the next stage rather than continuing to keep it largely to myself.

Since then, a few schools and school principals have independently reached out about the project and its potential use with their students. I have not gone out looking for institutional adoption yet, so seeing that kind of interest this early has only reinforced for me that there may be something much larger here.

I am now reaching the point where one person is no longer enough.

What began as a largely one-man project needs to become a serious, properly structured effort with the people, technology, scholarship, and capital necessary to build it at the scale I think is possible.

I need builders who understand product, engineering, AI, data, and design; people deeply grounded in textual scholarship, languages, and the digital humanities; and people who understand early-stage projects, venture building, philanthropy, institutional partnerships, and funding ambitious ideas before they are fully obvious to everyone else.

I know quite a few people in those worlds happen to follow me here.

Rather than DMing or calling people out of the blue, I thought this was the more respectful way to open the door.

So if this is in your wheelhouse, or if over the years I have earned even an ounce of your trust or goodwill, please reach out privately.

And if this is not your field, but someone immediately comes to mind who I should be speaking with, I would be grateful for an introduction or a tag.

I would also appreciate people helping this reach beyond my immediate circle. If you have followed my work closely enough to speak to the seriousness of my scholarship, the way I approach texts and sources, or simply the degree to which I tend to obsess over these things, please feel free to RT or QT this and add your own thoughts. That kind of vouching would mean far more than anything I could say about myself.

I am intentionally keeping the details fairly close for now. There will be a time to talk publicly about exactly what I am building.

For the moment, I am looking for the right people.

If this sounds like something you should be part of, reach out. I would be very happy to show you what I have built, explain where I think it can go, and hear what you think.

We asked Nassim Alexandre (@GilgameshODs), Head of Onchain Asset Management and Curation at @RockawayX, about the recent vault growth, use cases and ongoing institutional adoption.

"Vaults are how products get pushed through large fintech platforms, and how different financial products get integrated onchain. Part of that is regulatory clarity. Part of it is that vault smart contracts are more battle-tested than they were. 

On the demand side, the comparison point for most users was a savings account paying far less. The risk profile is not the same, and that distinction matters, but the yield is higher, and that is what platforms are competing on. 

The questions we get have changed, too. It used to be whether we had a vault; now it is which vault we can bring, and how it can be built around their risk profile."

Zero starts with an advantage most new L1s don’t have.

They’ve spent years connecting 170+ chains, so they know exactly where the multi-chain setup creates friction.

That gives Zero a better starting point than most fresh L1s. But I wouldn’t call it a moat yet.

Still, knowing where other chains struggle doesn’t mean Zero will solve those problems better.

The bigger question for me is whether Zero can become more than a showcase for LayerZero tech.

LayerZero already works across the chains people use today. Zero now needs its own reason to exist, beyond simply having better interoperability.

Too early to say what will happen.

又一个被证伪的case：

刚看到一个新闻，雪球有个A 股投资大V叫U兄（关善祥）去世，40岁。

他2020年初还发了私募基金，三年以来亏损-60%以上。

有点震惊。

因为之前在雪球看过他的文章，后来还买过他写的一本书，讲价值投资的，觉得还可以，属于值得看一遍，但不值得看三遍的那种。

印象很深的是后来他讲投资是个长期事业，要活到120岁，所以非常注重饮食、锻炼、睡眠、空气和水的质量。

所以9月28日下午3点基金发公告说去世（图1），大概率不是什么疾病或猝死，而是主动自杀。

You'll all be familiar with memes pumping real Penny Stonks, but not manipulating in game economies...

$RSTR is attempting to build a MicroStrategy-style treasury, except the reserve asset is Robin Hood hats inside Old School RuneScape

author: defidave
quoted_text:
How Does UFG Treasury v1 Work?

Treasury v1 is the first immutable primitive of the UFG ecosystem. It receives fees from the ETH/UFG trading pair from @ponsdotfamily which the treasury accrues in ETH.

The $UFG token is a direct claim on the treasury. If a holder decides to redeem, they can enact a redemption against the treasury. Once this redemption is initiated, the $UFG they send is burned. In return, they receive ETH with the exception of a 2% exit fee which is returned back to the treasury.

What makes this mechanism so powerful is that it creates a permanent rising floor of ETH while the supply of $UFG becomes inherently deflationary.

Treasury v1 only holds ETH. It has no owner, no pause, no upgrades, and it is never actively managed. Its beauty lies in its simplicity with $UFG at the center of it all, being the beneficiary of present and future revenue streams. 

That being said... be prepared for major updates coming soon.

text:
Neat!

With proper testing, "genetic nurture" effects on kids' measured cognitive ability appear to fizzle out, and the effects of kids' PGS are large and direct.

Also, there's evidence of a Wilson effect: a person's own PGS predicts more with age. Their parents' doesn't. https://t.co/p79InfosMO
author: cremieuxrecueil
quoted_text:
Excited to share our work on genetic nurture, where we find that parental genetic liabilities associated with educational attainment appear unlikely to exert a large genetic nurture effect on childhood cognitive performance.

Preprint: https://t.co/SuGwcLzXdc

To reach this conclusion, we addressed a statistical problem in trio-based polygenic score regressions widely used in human genetics. In these, one regresses the child’s outcome on the child’s, mother’s, and father’s polygenic scores, and associations with parental PGSs are often interpreted as suggestive evidence that parental genotypes influence the child through the environment (genetic nurture).

However, assortative mating on the PGS trait can induce “phantom genetic nurture” in this design, as previously described by @AlexTISYoung and others. Intuitively, this occurs because PGSs are noisy and incomplete, leaving much of the genetic liability they target unobserved. One parental PGS can ‘tag’ the other’s genetic liability, which in turn tags some of the child’s genetic liability not captured by the PGS. Thus, a parental PGS association in the trio regression could simply reflect the child’s genetic liability influencing their trait.

To address this, we developed RAVEL (Recovering Assortment-adjusted Variance Explained by genetic Liabilities). RAVEL uses two independently constructed PGSs for the same trait. Both noisily index the same underlying genetic liability, but their estimation errors are independent. Under explicit assumptions, this design allows us to recover assortment-adjusted associations of the child’s and parents’ latent genetic liabilities with the child’s outcome. In simulations, RAVEL recovers the target effects well across the settings we examine.

For the empirical analysis, we used >30,000 complete trios in the MoBa cohort to assess whether parental genetic liabilities for educational attainment (EA) show evidence of genetic nurture effects on childhood cognitive performance. With standard trio PGS regression, we find, as others have, that the parental PGSs together explain ~10% as much variance as the child’s PGS (excluding covariances).

However, after applying RAVEL, the maternal association attenuates completely, but a small, significant paternal association remained, with the parental liabilities inferred to explain less than 0.5% as much variance as the child’s.

In short, the standard analysis suggests a potentially meaningful genetic nurture effect, whereas the assortment-adjusted analysis suggests that any remaining EA-related nurture effect on childhood cognitive performance is likely very small.

Much more in the paper, including evidence for a possible maternal effect on preterm birth, sibling IBD regressions, and differential parental associations at the phenotype tails. We are significantly expanding the analyses before journal submission, so feedback is welcome! I am extremely grateful to Olivia, Laura, Alexandra, @hfsunde, and @hilsomartin for their contributions to this work.

author: ryanberckmans
quoted_text:
I want to close my chapter, for now, on the EIP-8363 analysis. After having a few more calls with people who are for- and against- issuance reduction (stakers, founders, DeFi people, and regular Ethereum holders) - here is a subjective view on the matter. I think it has some new aspects I didn't see much of before (💡)

- TLDR 1: I don't think this should go through right now. The proposal is raw and the arguments are still weak. It's weird to say this because it has been in the works for five years on and off, but it still doesn't make sense. I respect the authors who put time and effort into this, but after looking into it and having so many conversations across the space - it doesn't check out.
- TLDR 2: Neither side should be talking about anyone being "captured." You cannot say that core devs living and breathing the network are captured. No, they care about it and are involved. That is good! Similarly, you cannot say DeFi founders or the staking companies are captured. These people own the asset and are economically interested in having it grow. We have to put those arguments aside - it is just cheap talk.
- TLDR 3: Regarding the process: whether now or later, issuance policy shouldn't just go through a normal network upgrade process. It's not just about repricing or a minor technical tweak; this is way too big to be considered in that fashion. Maybe it could work within the existing process, but only if the opinions of founders and other stakeholders were respected a bit more, rather than just discarding them all as being captured.

Now to the arguments 🦞

I haven't really strayed from what I wrote a few weeks ago (tweet below). As a shorter summary, the argument for reduction falls through three main holes.

1. First, there is this allegiance to a "no inflation" economy perception: the idea that inflation is inherently bad, that (over)paying for something is bad, and that there is just too much of something. That mindset is not correct. In the modern economic world, since we stopped making money only from growing potatoes, it doesn't make sense. The belief that this will somehow make the Ethereum price moon, or that there is too much ETH being dumped on the market, is nonsense. It's one of the least inflating assets.

💡 You have to consider your broader goals. Your issuance strategy should reflect your general adoption strategy. If you think ETH is just an asset, money, a unit of account, or whatever narrative you want to come up with - like the "pet rock" meme Bitcoin style - fine. It's not bad, and it's okay to say that. But then the general adoption strategy should reflect it. It should just be marketing a hard asset, not worry about devs, open-source or anything creative. It's just digital gold, go to hard money conferences and enjoy.

However, if you see Ethereum as a World Computer, as a way to build different use cases, as an "infinite garden" for lack of a better phrase, as a platform - then there is no point in cutting the issuance. Currently, issuance creates different opportunities and products on this platform. EVEN IF you think it's a subsidy, then what? Platforms have subsidies. Why tamper with it if you have no definite alternative. These subsidies worked, they continue working and getting attention, and the platform is winning as a result of that (adoption, liquidity, trust, security, etc.)

If you offboard one big user segment from your marketplace, what's your alternative? Because you are then killing some of the plants in your garden that you've previously incentivized. It's not a weed, and presenting it as a weed is incorrect because nothing shows that's the case.

2. Second, the argument falls through on all the talk about the staking ratio, staking centralization, supply capture, solo stakers, inability to pass slashing, and so on. These are generally good discussions to have, but the suggested proposal does not fix those 🚫

💡 Take the part about slashing and forks, for example. All of these fancy ideas of how staker behavior is going to play out aren't really realistic. Nobody writes about which network - in terms of a slashing event or a fork - USDC, USDT, and centralized issuers would actually consider and back. 

Important factors affecting network resilience should be solved, but this proposal does not solve them. It does not improve conditions for solo stakers. The argument that the staking distribution will get worse if we continue - is also unproven. There is no proper distinction made between "good" LSTs and "bad" LSTs (if you want to think this way). If you believe that Binance and Coinbase staking shouldn't be increasing as much, that's a different discussion. A blanket cut wouldn't kill them as much as it would kill some LSTs that are actually favorable to the development of the core network. I'm not against an issuance reduction as a move potentially; I'm against how it is being argued, and that it's being argued in a weak way .

3. Third, the mechanics of yield are now being accepted as an asset in DeFi protocols (stETH over raw ETH, for example). These are interesting opportunities to consider, but thinking you can mess with this in isolation while killing what exists now isn't cool. Having Ethereum's economic policy be more set in stone is far more important to current participants than just trying out stuff by breaking an ecosystem that exists today.

💡 If institutions and such players appreciate ETH as an asset and engage with real use cases, do not stop them by trying to hypothetically make other use cases possible. They appreciate the current staking rate and have built strategies around it. 

If the proposal would solve security or network resilience while causing some pain in the short term, that would be acceptable. But as I've established, the arguments presented are weak and in many cases incorrect, so it doesn't even solve the purpose.

-----

You have to decide what you actually want to happen:

- Do you want to play trader and mess around with the ETH price by thinking less inflation is better
- Or do you want to solve network resilience and make it uncapturable?

You have to answer one of these questions. Right now, they are all packaged together. As a result, it's a mess, because it's not solving a problem that is explained - or it's solving a problem that is not proven to exist. 

Sorry 8363, but hope no.

text:
【Aave悄悄改了USDe基准借贷利率？低风险循环贷没得玩了？🙃】

整个中文CT估计忙着参与Robinhood/台湾未来祭FUTUREMODE，没什么人关注这个议题

主要是之前Pendle出了个PT AUTOLOOP 功能，我就塞进去做PT-sUSDe(Plasma)循环贷，原本吃15%APY

结果这两天看，woc被反撸啦😭😭😭然后就哭着去了解来龙去脉。。。

=====来龙去脉分割线=====
众所周知USDe是稳定币，持有者不会得到利息，但可以零成本Stake成sUSDe（年化～4.5%APY）

@aave 上 USDe的借贷曲线是沿用USDC/USDT的（base rate 0%，实际借贷利率看使用率utilization rate而定，一般在年化2.5%左右), 结果就很多人就存sUSDe，借USDe再质押，循环10次后年化>20%，风险也较低。

那么问题来了，为什么Aave上可以借到那么便宜的Usde？

其实就是Ethena用户在买单（或帮忙补贴）， 因为借来的USDe拿去质押分Ethena的收益，但那些USDe不是“新的钱”。等于一锅粥一样大，但来吃的人却越来越多

@Token_Logic 在Aave论坛上提出的proposal解决方案便是：把USDe的base rate 从0%拉上去5.25%， 分五六次在两周内实施完毕。

图一也能看到蓝线像楼梯一样逐渐上去，每个台阶都是aave risk steward在执行方案，然后在9/5的时候穿过绿线（pt fixed apy)，我的PT autoloop也就GG了。

所以pt-susde loop是不是就死了？

没有，它只是换了条腿，例如你可以借GHO/USDT，杠杆拉满依然有10%年化以上。

===对Aave的影响===

V3的USDe借贷账本从8/17 的 544M掉到 9/7 的 295M，换来的是USDC/USDT债务+300M，但接盘的池子也开始满了，USDT 使用率94.3%， 超过Kink的话借贷利率会很贵。

好在Aave在V4对USDC放了2%补贴，V4借USDT的PT Loop也有19%APY。总体来说杠杆还在，但大家从V3跑去V4而已。DAO收入可能就哭哭了

===对Ethena的影响===

@ethena 收入 = Float（USDe流通量，收益总量与Float成正比）x Backing的收益率；目前来看USDe供给从提案公布到现在还增加了300M，只要Float没缩就代表收入没缩。

有意思的是，图二显示DeFi Lending占了30%，如果这一块有相当一部分供给在Aave的稳定币，那TokenLogic这个提案把22个市场的slope1加了50bps，等于直接抬高了Ethena自己backing的收益，所以这个提案可能通过两条路推高sUSDe收益：
A）干掉循环贷，把吃大锅饭的人减少
B）抬高Aave提供利率让Ethena的Lending Sleeve赚更多
（但这个只是个假设，有待日后证实，还有比较尴尬的是Ethena分别在五条链上还有Looping Required的Merkl补贴😗）

===对Pendle的影响===

借USDe的杠杆跑了，PT-sUSDe（PLASMA）从4.8%升到了5.37%，PT买压跑了对一般散户也有好处，如果风险偏好保守的其实5.3%的年化（像做45天的定期存款，池子10/22到期）也不错。

项目目前收取的是PT swap fee + PT Looping service fee，例如一个 10 倍 loop 的成本：$1M 本金买 $10M PT，swap fee 约 $10K，service fee 约 $5K，合计 1.5% of 本金、0.15% of notional。平仓只有 swap fee，约 0.10%。来回大概 0.25% of notional。目前看起来没什么人主动Unloop，有的话也只是换了条腿（Aave V4）去借钱吧。看下来对Pendle的影响总体不大。

===

数据可能有出入，欢迎各路英雄指教，TLDR的话就是这个提案对Ethena的影响是中性偏正面。

text:
i used to think consumer apps were dead.

why would i need an app to book a flight if i could just text an AI to search and book on my behalf?

it seemed so obvious that everything i use my computer for could be done with text or voice. this was a hill i was willing to die on.

i've completely changed my opinion. 

the problem is that a conversation is a terrible interface for everything.

chat apps are a UI paradigm shift that genuinely feels like a miracle. you can give an app a messy, multimodal input: say something, type something, take a photo. 

and the app turns that into intent. it understands you.

but the output is more language for you to consume, correct, and steer.

it turns intent into more work. every text response creates another job and a decision. 

the best consumer apps have spent decades learning how to ask the user for less.

but a chat asks for more.

imagine using uber in a chat:

"where would you like to go?"
"i found several possible destinations."
"would you prefer the cheaper ride or the faster one?"
"your driver is seven minutes away. would you like me to proceed?"

uber is clearly a better product because it compresses all of these decisions into a single question: 

"where are you going?"

we've confused intent with a conversation when the output should instead be, like uber, the desired outcome.

a calorie tracker shouldn't talk to you about your lunch. it should log it.

a shopping app shouldn't give you a paragraph about what to buy. it should build the cart.

a travel app shouldn't interview you. it should give you the itinerary.

before ai, software had to anticipate how users would express intent: buttons, forms, menus, filters, queries.

now the input can be literally anything.

the next wave of consumer apps is what happens after your intent is understood.

This is insane! People's imagination for using memeFi is hitting new levels

You'll all be familiar with memes pumping real Penny Stonks, but not manipulating in game economies...

$RSTR is attempting to build a MicroStrategy-style treasury, except the reserve asset is Robin Hood hats inside Old School RuneScape

Why now? Because it's on Robonhood chain...

How it works:

1) $RSTR launched on pons against ETH
2) Every trade pays a 1% fee; of which 70% accrue to the token creator + 30% to pons
3) The RSTR operator claims the creator fees, converts the ETH into OSRS gold (assuming through Bond purchases?) uses that gold to buy Robin Hood hats
4) The hats are spread across multiple RuneScape accounts + withheld from sale
5) Removing hats from circulation pushes up the in-game market price, generating screenshots, attention and theoretically more $RSTR trading
6) More $RSTR trading produces more creator fees, funding further hat purchases

I wanted to check this against a third party source to see if this was actually happening... it is!

i) The GE tracker most players use in RuneScape is showing a spike from 700k RSGP to 4.5m now each hat in just two days
ii) The current price you can buy the hats for is > $4.5m RSGP... i checked and max bid to buy more of the supply actually in game (screenshot)

The main challenges to the process is that there's an element that needs to be off-chain with a human intermediary in using the ETH fees to purchase bonds + then in game currency for the RH hats

I'm not a lawyer but as long as they're purchasing the bonds through Jagex then it should be in compliance? Although not sure about intentional manipulation of in game economics?

Even so... if the accounts are banned it permanently removes the hats from the game and hence achieves the same outcome

You can capitalize on this by buying in game before it goes insane or more speculative through their token

Jagex would receive the revenue from Bond sales, but it's not public so we are unable to benefit from that side of the trade

Once again onchain mechanisms being used with memes to draw in more retail attention... this time from millions of RuneScape players!

quoted_text:
@grok, build the evidence base for the model agreement @mcuban is proposing.

First figure out whether “the contract” is actually a stack of agreements covering development, tax incentives, zoning, power, water, community benefits, and enforcement, with different public bodies controlling different pieces.

Find agreements data centers have actually signed with U.S. cities, counties, states, utilities, and other public bodies. Use the executed documents wherever possible, not articles describing them.

Compare what communities gave up with what they received, especially taxes and subsidies, power and grid costs, water, jobs, infrastructure, environmental obligations, community payments, reporting, audits, guarantees, clawbacks, penalties, expansion, ownership changes, and decommissioning.

For each protection, tell us:

• the strongest version a company actually agreed to
• who has authority to enforce it
• how the community can verify compliance
• what happens if the company fails
• the loopholes weaker versions leave open

Keep proven terms separate from good ideas nobody has accepted yet.

Then use the evidence to build a modular model term sheet, organized by which public body controls each part, plus a negotiation guide showing where communities have leverage and which obligations need to be signed before approvals are granted.

The test is simple: a protection should be enforceable, measurable, and attached to someone with the authority to act when it’s violated.

End by showing what separates real community protection from a promise that only sounds protective. Reply in Plain English for readers.

quoted_text:
🚀 Sol-H3: @MiniMax_AI H3 Video Generation Faster Than Playback 🤩

Five seconds of world. 1.653 seconds to infer.

We’re releasing Sol-H3, our fastest end-to-end MiniMax-H3 inference stack yet. On one 8× NVIDIA B300 Blackwell system, it generates five seconds of 1344×768 video with stereo audio in 1.653 seconds. Across 1×, 4×, and 8× B300, Sol-H3 reaches up to a 15.54× speedup versus Base H3.

Compared with 50-step Base H3 Dense on the same 8× B300 system, the four-step Sol-H3 profile delivers:
• 5s: 18.250s → 1.653s (11.04×)
• 10s: 50.660s → 3.732s (13.57×)
• 15s: 99.513s → 6.612s (15.05×)

Sol-H3 also scales across GPU counts:
• 4× B300: 2.918s / 6.993s / 12.542s for 5s / 10s / 15s (12.11–15.54×)
• 1× B300: 13.745s / 37.813s / 52.260s for 5s / 10s / 15s (9.45–14.29×)

All figures are medians of three measured runs after one warmup at 1344×768 and 24 FPS with stereo audio. Base H3 uses 50 scheduler points (49 DiT forwards); Sol-H3 uses four DiT forwards, so this is a full-profile comparison—not an attention-only runtime change. Sol-H3 uses Dense attention on 1× B300 and SOL with INT8 QKV / FP8 output transport on 4× / 8×. Timing includes text encoding, DiT denoising, and video/audio VAE decoding; model loading, compilation warmup, and final MP4 encoding are excluded.

Sol-H3 brings Sol-Engine × Sol-Attn into one full-stack runtime:
• dynamic sparse attention with no retraining
• fused norm, RoPE, MLP, and sparse-attention setup
• fused INT8 QKV / FP8 output communication across 8 GPUs
• parallel, batched VAE decoding
• precomputed AdaLN caching

Inside the stack:
• sparse-attention setup: 1.206 → 0.285 ms (−76.4%)
• VAE decode: 7.55 → 0.602 s
• ~24 GB memory freed per GPU

Any MiniMax-H3 few-step LoRA can plug into the same engine, and the code is deployment-friendly under Apache 2.0.

For us, the bigger milestone is crossing from “fast generation” into “faster than playback.” That opens the path toward continuous 24 FPS generation and truly interactive video systems.

We’re excited to partner with @reactorworld to release Sol-H3 and make it available as an API day-0.

author: MiniMax_AI
quoted_text:
🚀 Sol-H3: @MiniMax_AI H3 Video Generation Faster Than Playback 🤩

Five seconds of world. 1.653 seconds to infer.

We’re releasing Sol-H3, our fastest end-to-end MiniMax-H3 inference stack yet. On one 8× NVIDIA B300 Blackwell system, it generates five seconds of 1344×768 video with stereo audio in 1.653 seconds. Across 1×, 4×, and 8× B300, Sol-H3 reaches up to a 15.54× speedup versus Base H3.

Compared with 50-step Base H3 Dense on the same 8× B300 system, the four-step Sol-H3 profile delivers:
• 5s: 18.250s → 1.653s (11.04×)
• 10s: 50.660s → 3.732s (13.57×)
• 15s: 99.513s → 6.612s (15.05×)

Sol-H3 also scales across GPU counts:
• 4× B300: 2.918s / 6.993s / 12.542s for 5s / 10s / 15s (12.11–15.54×)
• 1× B300: 13.745s / 37.813s / 52.260s for 5s / 10s / 15s (9.45–14.29×)

All figures are medians of three measured runs after one warmup at 1344×768 and 24 FPS with stereo audio. Base H3 uses 50 scheduler points (49 DiT forwards); Sol-H3 uses four DiT forwards, so this is a full-profile comparison—not an attention-only runtime change. Sol-H3 uses Dense attention on 1× B300 and SOL with INT8 QKV / FP8 output transport on 4× / 8×. Timing includes text encoding, DiT denoising, and video/audio VAE decoding; model loading, compilation warmup, and final MP4 encoding are excluded.

Sol-H3 brings Sol-Engine × Sol-Attn into one full-stack runtime:
• dynamic sparse attention with no retraining
• fused norm, RoPE, MLP, and sparse-attention setup
• fused INT8 QKV / FP8 output communication across 8 GPUs
• parallel, batched VAE decoding
• precomputed AdaLN caching

Inside the stack:
• sparse-attention setup: 1.206 → 0.285 ms (−76.4%)
• VAE decode: 7.55 → 0.602 s
• ~24 GB memory freed per GPU

Any MiniMax-H3 few-step LoRA can plug into the same engine, and the code is deployment-friendly under Apache 2.0.

For us, the bigger milestone is crossing from “fast generation” into “faster than playback.” That opens the path toward continuous 24 FPS generation and truly interactive video systems.

We’re excited to partner with @reactorworld to release Sol-H3 and make it available as an API day-0.

text:
The United Founders Group $UFG Thesis 🏛️

$UFG an onchain ETH treasury that pays you to hold via multiple revenue streams. It has the potential to be the $YFI of this cycle; it is truly novel in its mechanics yet simple in its design.

Each $UFG token is first and foremost 98% redeemable for ETH in its treasury. The other 2% is an exit fee that is sent back into the treasury, creating a permanent rising floor of the ETH in it. The $UFG treasury is an immutable contract that is not controlled by anyone.

Because of its tokenomics of having a fixed supply of 1 billion that burns $UFG every time that ETH is redeemed from the treasury, making the token deflationary. So now you inherently have this interesting conflux of ETH in the treasury perpetually increasing while $UFG supply constantly decreases.

The first revenue stream of $UFG are 100% of the creator fees from $UFG's own market on @ponsdotfamily. Anyone can call this contract to collect for the treasury and in the future, the contract can collect revenue streams from future products and primitives. And while many new tokens are pairing to untested onchain stocks, $UFG is pairing to the most tried and tested decentralized finance asset there is, ETH.

This comes to why I like $UFG so much. It is because it is fair. I believe that we are seeing a swing back to PvE this cycle where holding and contributing will be rewarded while paper hands will be punished. $PONS was the first to prove this, building a launchpad that rewards creators with fees and holders with buybacks. What launches like $UFG prove is that $PONS isn't just for memecoins but for real DeFi primitives looking to launch in a fair manner and those that build in this spirit will win.

On the roadmap, the next revenue stream is options with the first asset being tokenized-SPY exposure. How it works is there are two tokens, a "Buffer token" a which holds a 10% loss in exchange for a capped upside. The "Writer token" is the inverse, it posts the collateral that absorbs the losses and is only paid in the upside goes beyond the Buffer cap. Both tokens fund themselves purely from their own trading fees, take no deposits, and route a fixed share of fees to the $UFG treasury. There will be more information about this product soon.

I've talked to the founder and multiple holders of $UFG and its success really depends on the people. We have an incredible opportunity here to build something that is in the spirit of DeFi but it can only happen if people believe that a better future is possible.

The flywheel is already in motion; more products -> more revenue streams -> more ETH accumulation -> more proving the power of DeFi, but to get it into turbo drive it can't be done alone. Not by me. Not by you. Not by any single person. It will have to be a group effort.

It is early and yes there are risks, but if you're reading and made it this fair there must be something within you that wants to take a chance.

The time has come to return to tradition. The time has come to return to PvE. The time has come for $UFG 🏛️

I talked about moving beyond naive prompting toward an agentic OS, and how eval-driven harness design can expose more of a model’s underlying capabilities through persistent computation, memory, and agent-to-agent communication.
author: harjtaggar
quoted_text:
Harnesses often get dismissed as just scaffolding, just prompt engineering, and not real research. But that couldn't be farther from the truth. The same model weights that score 30% on ARC-AGI score 95% with a better harness.

So we gathered a group of researchers and founders working at the frontier to do a deep dive into the state of harnesses. 

We cover how we got to this point, the case for making your harness as expressive as possible, and what YC learned building an agent for every employee in the company.

text:
I keep getting asked for a $LITE  post and a $COHR post.

okay, but let's walk the object first

an AI rack does not “need optics” the way a pitch deck needs a slide. It needs a working optical lane. 

That lane is a stack:

→ Indium / phosphorus chemistry 
→ InP substrate ($AXTI , Sumitomo, $IQE, Freiberger) 
→ epitaxy 
→ laser / EML / CW source ($LITE , $COHR, Sivers overflow, AAOI in the module path) 
→ engine or pluggable 
→ DSP / retimer fabric (Marvell, Broadcom, Credo, Astera) 
→ package and, soon enough, hybrid-bonded co-packaged optics (BESI’s station) 
→ the GPU 

Goldman style TAM slides will tell you CPO goes from roughly nothing to a very large number. 
some divergence still holds: US laser names carry pluggable books that can get cannibalised. 

The cleaner move on paper is often one layer up, where there is nothing to cannibalize, SOI for silicon photonics, InP substrates, the bonders that put light onto the package.

This week’s desk noise fits that map. Bloomberg language on IQE: indium phosphide substrates as a key risk for the semiconductor industry. 
LITE’s CEO: InP tighter than memory. 
COHR: eating its own InP into 800G/1.6T while 6-inch capacity and a CPO calendar approach.

The hidden gem is not another “optics supercycle” headline.

It is this:

- silicon cannot lase
- lasers need crystal
- crystal supply is thin

Everything above that layer is a customer of a furnace cycle measured in weeks, not a software release measured in days.

Nov 27, 2026 still sits on the wall for China’s gallium / germanium / antimony control pause. If that flips, substrate names feel it before anybody books a dollar of CPO revenue.

The chain deserves to be walked, station by station.

Dashboard link if you want the live layer map: https://t.co/NW2xPxrf0p

Educational, not investment advice.

text:
Your mint function calls a stranger before it finishes counting your own supply.

Every safeMint contains a callback. The recipient contract gets notified it received a token, and for one moment execution control leaves your contract and lands in code someone else wrote. In a batch mint, that call fires inside your loop, while supply counters and per wallet limits are mid update.

If your state is not settled before that call goes out, the recipient can walk right back in.

It shows up in three shapes.

Straight reentry, the same function calls out and gets called back into before it finishes.

Cross function reentrancy, a second function shares state with the first, so guarding one function does nothing if the other is left open.

Read only reentrancy, an outside contract reads your state mid transaction, while it is temporarily wrong, and makes a decision based on a lie.

The rule: settle every counter, balance, and limit before you hand control to anyone else's code. Checks, effects, interactions, in that order, every time.

If you cannot say with certainty what your view functions report while a transaction is in flight, that is the finding.

text:
Thoughts on the Liquid whitehat incident:

Background:

- Liquid is a Bitcoin L2/sidechain, launched by Blockstream in 2018. 4,000 BTC from their bridge was taken by a whitehat yesterday (and then mostly returned).

- You can think of the Liquid network as running a fork of Bitcoin Core (called Elements). Elements added new features such as confidential transactions, other assets, BTC peg in/out, and new opcodes.

- The bug seems not to be a cryptography one but in integration logic. Bug A was there for years, was recently patched, and the patch likely introduced Bug B, which was exploited.

- I’m glad this was a whitehat, and most of the funds have been returned. Could’ve been much worse if an actual attacker.

Learnings: 

- There should’ve been rate limits in place both at the swap service and peg out. There likely were some limits that didn’t trigger. Such rate limits and time delays can drastically reduce the potential damage.

- It’s clear that we’re in the age of AI-driven security wars. The new capability of these models is forcing us to discover bugs that went undetected for years. Overall, this will be a net positive, even if short-term painful.

- Both the earlier Zcash bug and this Liquid one reinforce how keeping Bitcoin simple and hardened is the right call. If anything, we should be pushing for Bitcoin ossification.

Stacks security:

- I got several questions about Stacks. We also have a bridge for sBTC. The exact Elements bug isn't applicable here, as Stacks doesn’t use Elements. For any bridges or DeFi apps, security should be priority #1. Stacks devs actively run frontier AI models (both open-source and from frontier labs) on our repos. We also have active bug bounty programs with Immunefi and others. Our regular security audit reports are also available publicly.

- Even with the emphasis on security, AI model testing, audits, etc, for over a year, Stacks devs have been pushing in the long-term direction of self-custodial solutions. The Bitcoin bonds/staking upgrade keeps the BTC deployed fully self-custodial (no bridge or smart contract risk). Further, new approaches to self-custodial lending and other areas are in the R&D stage right now.

Summary: 

Running the absolute latest AI models on sensitive repos is job #1 for crypto devs. We’ll see a short-term increase in discovered bugs but get hardened systems and healthy practices in the long term.

Stacks is now heavily focusing on self-custodial solutions for bitcoin capital markets, while relentlessly doing defensive security testing/audits on existing infra.

The Liquid incident should be a wake-up call to take AI threats extremely seriously, even at Bitcoin Core (we’ve done some work on this). We should ossify Bitcoin Core and keep it as simple as possible; all new bitcoin functionality can be built on layers like Stacks. Forward!

2021 and 2022 were quiet, but I was having fun.

Building something people finally paid for and enjoyed made me so happy.

My first 5 years of failures taught me not to get emotionally attached to a project, because everything goes to 0 eventually.

So I just kept shipping.

It's 2026, and I've launched 36 startups.

Only 11% made decent money.

Back in 2016, when I started, I believed I would make it.

If I had known it would take 7 years of failure, I probably would never have started.

That's why I'm stupidly optimistic.

I don't think in years. I don't dream big.

I think in weeks. I build tiny projects fast. And I quit even faster.

That's how I wake up happy, enjoy the journey, and eventually build life-changing projects.
