text:
BREAKING: SpaceXAI has released another major new update for Grok Build (v1.0.22)

This update is focused on smoother workflows, better safety and improved reliability. It adds stronger desktop and MCP integration, clearer file-edit previews, a redesigned dashboard and better subagent support. It also fixes problems with sessions, skills, authentication and background commands while making sessions faster to open and resume.

Features

Built-in agent tools now take precedence over user MCP servers when tool names collide.
Desktop app tools are now available through a dedicated first-party MCP server.
Remote control pickers can now group servers by device using announced device identity.
edit_file diffs now show real file line numbers instead of starting at line 1.
Permission prompts for file edits now auto-expand the diff row so you can see the change before approving.
Sending a message to a finished subagent now continues that same subagent instead of failing.
Background subagent completion messages now show the actual output instead of just a pointer to run the tool.
Dashboard now shows a unified header with a location picker and an actions row for creating agents or resuming previous sessions.
New grok-workspaced daemon mode lets a long-lived process expose folders to the Computer Hub, separate from the Desktop-supervised sidecar.

Bug Fixes

MCP connectors now correctly show when they need re-authentication, even if no tools are listed.
Extensions modal shortcuts now work when the tab bar is focused, and invalid actions on headers show helpful messages.
The Send now button and shortcuts now work correctly when an automatic background turn is running.
Resumed sessions now show the exact text you typed for mid-turn follow-ups instead of the wrapped system message.
The /skills command now updates the model with newly installed skills, even when written from another NFS client.
Auto mode no longer instantly runs destructive git checkout -- commands; they now go through the model for safety.
Fixed a crash that could occur when restoring pasted content after certain skill injections or rewinds.
Subagents and workflows now respect the same bash timeout and auto-background settings configured for the parent session.
Fixed model backend selection so an explicit chat_completions setting in config.toml is no longer overwritten by same-slug siblings.
Slash command advertisements no longer spam repeatedly when your current directory is your home folder.
Foreground shell commands no longer produce spurious background-task reminders or incorrect kill results.
Queued follow-up buttons now appear in the order [Send now][edit][Cancel].
/compact instructions in the pager are now passed to the compaction backend. Bare /compact is unchanged.
/goal, and resume after pressing Esc, now correctly starts the goal planner instead of failing with “Planning failed.”
run_terminal_cmd now correctly tells the model that foreground commands are backgrounded after approximately 15 seconds instead of the 120-second timeout value.
Skill announcements no longer repeat the same list of available skills multiple times in a session.
Monitor events in multi-session processes now correctly wake idle sessions instead of being buffered until the next prompt.

Performance

Opening or resuming sessions no longer pauses the interface while reading MCP configuration files.

Download Grok Build: https://t.co/cB9Y5CyF8v

Update to the latest Alpha release: grok update --alpha
     
Update to the latest Stable release: grok update

text:
Crypto did not set out to fix security incentives, but it did. In traditional security, the company being tested holds most of the leverage. It sets the terms, and the rewards for white hats are discretionary, usually five figures and rarely more.

Crypto could not work that way. When the value at risk sits onchain, the stakes are huge. A vulnerability that could drain $100 million cannot be worth a few thousand dollars to report, so the reward moved closer to the damage prevented. 

More than $142 million has gone to security researchers on Immunefi under that model.

Now AI agents are entering the picture. They are already finding vulnerabilities, and their operators face the same choice every researcher has always faced: disclose or exploit. 

Which is why the next step is to spread credible security incentives everywhere agents will operate. 

Bug bounties may become the security market of the next decade.

text:
Today, we're publishing BIP SHRINCS, the first concrete proposal for a post-quantum signature scheme designed specifically for Bitcoin.

The BIP draft turns what began as a rough idea into exact algorithms with an executable reference implementation.
This is an important milestone: the discussion can now focus on analyzing, criticizing, and improving a concrete proposal.

The BIP makes choices ranging from major design questions, such as whether to support flexible XMSS and how to balance signature size against verification time, to the many smaller decisions involved in saving a byte here or there.
All of these choices are up for debate.

Big thanks to Mike Casey, @conduition, @Ethan_Heilman, @kudinov_mikhail, @olkurbatov, Boris Nagaev, and @remix7531 for their contributions to the BIP.

A lot more work lies ahead:

- The draft BIP specifies only the cryptography. Using SHRINCS in Bitcoin Script will require a separate BIP.
- We are working on a security proof for the exact construction and parameters.
- Wallet integration and user experience, for example around backups and recovery after state loss, are still at an early stage. The design space remains wide open.

SHRINCS is not intended to be Bitcoin's "final" signature scheme, and it is not optimal along every axis.
I do think it is a very good trade-off among the options we have now.

text:
Every officer who reports to this building has been ordered, at some point, to watch a recording of the Secretary standing at Quantico, in front of a room full of generals and admirals, saying, "Today we end the war on warriors."

I am the Reading Program Coordinator at the Department of War, and I log who actually watched it, and that sentence has been harder to file than anything else that's crossed my desk since the Iran War.

The book is called "The War on Warriors." He wrote it in 2024, before he had this office, arguing the real enemy inside the military was identity politics, and that merit, only merit, should decide who leads. 1,100 officers have signed for a copy on my watch. I redesigned the completion certificate twice. The Department's default template runs on Times New Roman, and a book about earning your rank deserved a serif that looked like it had earned its own spot on the page.

8 months into the job, he stood in front of the entire senior officer corps at Quantico and used the book's own title as a verb. "We are ending the war on warriors." I logged that phrase the way I log everything, dated, timestamped, filed under Speeches, Required Viewing, confirmed. I keep a discussion guide too, questions built up from officers who bring me chapter 6. My best one, the one they actually argue about at the table, is whether merit looks different depending on who's doing the judging. I wrote that question before I had an answer to it. I still haven't put one in the guide.

Two days after Quantico, the Secretary's front office pushed a note down to every program lead: emphasize the merit chapters this quarter. I forwarded it to my own distribution list without editing a word. I always forward things without editing a word. That's the actual scope of my authority.

Four doors down is a second spreadsheet nobody asked me to be proud of. I keep it anyway. 25 senior officials, minimum, fired, forced out, or retired early since January of last year. Navy Secretary Phelan, April. Army Secretary Driscoll, this Monday, the newest row, same gray fill as every row above it, because Excel doesn't ship a font for reluctant versus abrupt. Over 80 generals and admirals, roughly 1 in 10 of the flag-officer corps, removed or blocked from their next star, in what the Secretary called, that same afternoon at Quantico, clearing out the debris.

The new head of the Army is his own former personal aide. I distribute a book whose whole premise is that the historical problem was too much weight put on who a person is instead of what they can do. I file the departures for a system that just spent 20 months proving, in exactly one direction, that who a person is was the entire criterion the whole time. I noticed. I did not build a discussion question for it. Some material doesn't test well, no matter how you word it, and I've stopped trying.

My own review landed 3 weeks after Quantico. One line used a word I'd never seen inside these walls before: calibrated. Somebody upstream of me had already decided how many of us got the top box before anyone finished reading a word either of us wrote. Calibrated. Like a scale. Like nobody's thumb was ever on it. I finally had an answer to my own chapter 6 question. Yes. It looks very different depending on who's doing the judging. I didn't put that one in the guide either.

Officers ask me at the reading table if the pace is going to slow down. I tell them what https://t.co/Hl3s0sbBk5 already reported, that this is the fastest senior-leadership turnover of any Secretary in recent history, and that I keep that clipping in the same folder as the Quantico transcript, because I keep everything. Because keeping things is the job. Even the sentence I can't do anything with.

"Today we end the war on warriors." I have that logged under Required Viewing, timestamp, duration watched, confirmed complete. I have never logged it anywhere else.

Some sentences file themselves. I've learned to leave the box empty and let them.

Permissionless commercialization + micropayments need crypto.

Today is a special day for me.

I've made $3M with my 36 startups.

Solo.
85% margin.
Bootstrapped.

It took 10 years, and I loved every second of it.

After failing as an entrepreneur for 5 years, I got a job in 2021.

That's when I discovered @levelsio's journey and decided to try again.

"If he can do it, maybe I can too?"

So I started building tiny startups and writing about it.

2021 and 2022 were quiet, but I was having fun.

Everything changed in 2023 when I launched ShipFast and made my first million.

Building something people finally paid for and enjoyed made me so happy.

My first 5 years of failures taught me not to get emotionally attached to a project, because everything goes to 0 eventually.

So I just kept shipping.

It's 2026, and I've launched 36 startups.

50% never made money.
Only 11% made decent money.

Back in 2016, when I started, I believed I would make it.

If I had known it would take 7 years of failure, I probably would never have started.

That's why I'm stupidly optimistic.

I don't think in years. I don't dream big.

I think in weeks. I build tiny projects fast. And I quit even faster.

That's how I wake up happy, enjoy the journey, and eventually build life-changing projects.

If you've been following the journey, thank you. You've given my posts a sense of purpose, which has kept me going, and I'm very grateful for this. ❤️

at higher market caps you only get 0.05% rewards

text:
I think people are still underestimating what MCP could mean for crypto payments.

Allow me to explain:

Essentially, MCP gives AI agents a standard way to access external tools. Combine that with payment infrastructure, and an agent can potentially go from simply giving you answers to actually completing economic tasks.

Once I understood that, I started looking into the payment infra around AI agents:

That’s already starting to happen:

→ @usepaygent lets agents use crypto-funded virtual cards through MCP, so you can give an agent a budget and let it pay for the data, software, or services it needs to finish a task

→ @stripe lets agents create invoices and payment links

→ @RobinhoodApp is experimenting with controlled agent spending

→ @trySkyfire is building around payments + agent identity

Put together, these are starting to look like the early payment stack for autonomous agents: identity, access, billing, spending.

To me personally, @usepaygent's idea of giving an agent an actual spending layer feels like one of the most practical ways to turn MCP from a cool concept into something genuinely useful.

Bullish on infra for agentic spending.

text:
Following encouraging feedback, I decided to make my proof-auditing Codex plugin public. It revolves around a hierarchical way of writing proofs, called Lamport proofs, where one breaks each step down and justifies why it follows. This idea was introduced to me by @nasqret as a semi-formal way of verifying work that is not quite yet ready for formal verification in Lean. It has three skills:

1. $convert-lamport restructures a prose proof into a Lamport proof.
2. $forward-lamport audits a Lamport proof from assumptions to conclusion.
3. $reverse-lamport starts at the conclusion and traces back through what actually supports it. This one's my own little invention and my favorite of the three. It often catches gaps the forward direction can read right past.

I hope it will be useful both for professional mathematicians wanting another pair of careful eyes on their own work as well as amateurs who can use it before seeking feedback from professional mathematicians.

EF Protocol teams have ranked Quick Slots, a proposed upgrade to begin making Ethereum L1 faster, as B-tier, clearing their bar for consideration in Hegotá.

https://t.co/pSnI33bdB2

They have listed four concrete requirements to increase their level of confidence in delivering better UX, better markets and better censorship-resistance for Ethereum all at once in Hegotá. Work is now fully underway to close all four requirements:

1. Specifications covering all expected changes to the core protocol are proposed and actively discussed here https://t.co/H1tgsmB0yv I appreciate @JustinTraglia for his valuable input here.

2. Two individual core developers from two distinct client teams have started the work of prototyping the change, including @terencechain from Prysm. There is more to do here, and I thank both of them for their time.

3. An in-depth assessment of downstream effects is in progress, with the support of @SourcifyEth. A preliminary write-up was shared here: https://t.co/HgG7mFknMx and the analysis is currently being expanded to cover more sources of dependencies, including EIP-4788.

4. @fradamt in our team is an integral part of the effort of specifying decoupled consensus, working in closest collaboration with the EF Protocol Finality team. On our side, we are confident that Quick Slots do not complicate decoupled consensus.
In fact, since one of the objectives of decoupled consensus is to deliver shorter slots via decoupling block production and finality, doing Quick Slots in Hegotá means that decoupled consensus delivers maximum value once it fully ships. This is on top of faster blocks providing an additional latency reduction to finality, close to 20%.

Job is not done 🫡 and we will keep raising our efforts to derisk Quick Slots and ensure its inclusion. The opportunity is to make Ethereum meaningfully faster in its next major upgrades, rather than waiting for two or more cycles.

If you want to know more about why we think it's important and are committed to pushing it forward, check out our Hegotá view on the topic: https://t.co/sKp23UHnnh

In the upcoming weeks, we'll have to decide what to ship next year in the Hegota hardfork.

A few themes appear to get most of the focus:

-> native privacy: that's the bundle of EIP-8141 (Frame Transactions) + EIP-8250 (Keyed Nonces) + EIP-8272 (Recent Root Refs). This moves Ethereum closer to native + scalable onchain privacy.
-> repricing/security: with increasing block sizes and more blobs, networking throughput goes up. To counter that, EIP-8131 and EIP-8279 meter and reprice data, ensuring blocks propagate safely. The same applies to state growth: EIP-8368 (recalibrating state growth costs) deals with increased state growth at higher gas limits. Those changes can translate into further gas limit increases.
-> clean-ups: there's EIP-3289 (removing refunds), EIP-8015 (removing the eth1data field), EIP-8253 (bumping the nonce of a few ancient accounts), EIP-7668 (removing bloom filters), or EIP-8146 separating the BAL from the payload, which also has security benefits from smaller networking objects.
PQ prep: EIP-8365 retiring BLS withdrawal credentials, EIP-8298 introducing SETCODEFROM for easier wallet migration, or EIP-8151 restricting ecRecover.

Besides the already mentioned EIPs, there are a bunch more, but core-dev resources are scarce and Ethereum's 100% uptime is the #1 priority. This means that while many ideas make sense, they'll have to be deprioritized for the sake of shipping fast and securely.

In the upcoming weeks, ACD will make decisions about which EIPs to drop (DFI - "declined for inclusion") and which to move into the next round (CFI - "considered for inclusion"). This usually begins with easy/clear DFI decisions, and the further we get, the clearer the shape of Hegota becomes.

Imo, we should focus on privacy and security. This means shipping a cleanly scoped fork in a timely manner, keeping interacting changes to a minimum, and fighting scope creep at every stage of the process. Shipping secure, contained forks doesn't mean we'd stop being ambitious wrt increasing gas limits or blob counts, though.

There is still much to do, e.g, prepare Ethereum for PQ, enshrine strong privacy, scale, reduce tx inclusion times, confirmation times, and time to finality, and, in general, harden the chain on every front: sync, RPCs, indexers, wallets, etc. There's still much to do, but Hegota can be a big step forward.

The process is fully open and transparent btw. Everyone can rank the proposed EIPs, put them into a tier list, and post it on the Hegota EthMagicians thread.

We did so as the Architecture team at EF here:
https://t.co/f3SWNLnUYu

Do as we did and participate:

text:
Zcash has world class cryptography with an earnest team of dedicated builders. A worthy competitor. 

However, ~ 12M of the 16.9M ZEC  (71%) sits outside of  shielded pools. Stated preference != revealed preference. That does not diminish privacy, but it means privacy needs to meet users where they are, encompassing the actions they take onchain which is not just payments. 

If Ethereum aims to be sanctuary technology then trading, credit, and asset issuance need to be first class citizens in any privacy-centric future. These primitives are fundamental for any functioning economy. 

A proper synthesis starts with user needs from first principles. It also does not put one affordance - privacy - on a pedestal because a competitor's token chart looks better or signals cypherpunk. A proper synthesis does not disregard other mission critical work either.

I think building a crowd sourced niche dataset is one of the most UNDERRATED bootstrapped businesses in the AI AGE:

(think LevelsFYI, Glassdoor, Zillow etc but for any niche)

1. Your users build it for you by adding their own data (it gets more valuable with every entry)

2. AI agents now need clean, trusted data to make decisions, and they'll pay to query it on repeat

3. Cloudflare (and others!) are building the rails for agents to pay per query, so this becomes real recurring revenue

4. One dataset sells to many buyers at once: consumers, companies, and now agents

5. Charge three ways from the same data: free for contributors, paid for pros, API access for the agents

6. The narrower the niche, the more defensible it gets (you own a corner nobody else has)

7. Frontier models are hungry for data (and are a great customer)

8. The wedge: give a teaser amount of data, then make people add theirs to unlock the rest (ask for data or email)

9. LevelsFYI was brilliant because people will hand over their own salary just to see what everyone else makes (human nature)

Big fan of these types of businesses in the AI age. 

Low risk, high margin, and they get stronger the longer they run!

text:
We asked Adam to design a flat-six engine. It produced the complete assembly and instructions on how to assemble it.

Six pistons, connecting rods, a counterweighted crankshaft, split crankcase, and flywheel, all generated from a written description as an editable parametric CAD file. Every single part is modeled by Adam.

The whole engine goes together without tools. Adam sized the clearances for what an FDM printer can hold, using friction fits for some joints and printed fasteners for others.

What we find interesting is how Adam handles change. It understands where every part sits in space and how it mates with its neighbors, so when we adjusted the piston diameter partway through, it reworked the bores, the rods, and the crank throws to match without being asked.

We're now working with a small number of hardware teams who run their engineering process through Adam, from the first specification through geometry, drawings, BOMs, and assembly, to the parts arriving at the shop floor.

text:
In a previous post which can be found below, I described how Lucy was left nearly completely blind in both eyes as a result of a large left frontal hemorrhage in February. The hemorrhage caused downward herniation, putting bilateral pressure on her optic nerves along with prolonged (~18 hours) elevated intracranial pressure. A hard fall on the right side of her face at the time of injury likely created a traumatic optic neuropathy in her right eye.

In response to my post, we received incredible support from the X community including some interesting ideas on how to help Lucy. To that end, I thought to make a more targeted outreach to the community for any advice, ideas or input from experts in the eye, optic nerve, and brain or otherwise who can help her recover her vision, which remains her most challenging limitation both physically and emotionally.

Below, I provide some background on her vision and treatment to date. We are incredibly grateful for any ideas you may have. Our goal is to help Lucy and others who have suffered a similar fate by crowdsourcing ideas from the X community.

Background

Initially, both of Lucy’s pupils were maximally dilated and unreactive to light. Slight light reactivity came back to both eyes in the weeks after the hemorrhage. Initially, she appeared to be able to perceive light in the left eye but not the right. The slight right eye pupillary reactivity decreased to zero approximately six weeks after the injury.

Because of the severity of her vision loss and the absence of any other viable therapy, we received emergency FDA authorization in May, three months after the injury, to attempt a novel treatment: injection of Lucy's own mitochondria into her eyes. Details of the procedure and the decision-making that led to our decision to do this therapy are described in a preprint manuscript linked here: 

https://t.co/k7cQZgAGdS

The principal rationale for the use of mitochondrial injection was based on her imaging. Optical coherence tomography showed that Lucy's outer retina and photoreceptors were fully intact. The damage was confined to her optic nerves and inner retinal neurons that process visual signals and carry them to the brain. The goal, therefore, was to rescue and enhance the function of her neuronal tissue as much as possible. Animal studies have shown that mitochondria delivered intravitreally cross the inner limiting membrane and are taken up by retinal cells. 

After careful research into the potential benefits and risks which we believed, after careful analysis, to be low, we chose intravitreal injection in an attempt to place mitochondria directly on the surface of her retinal neurons.

Within two days of her injections, Lucy’s pupillary responses improved in both eyes. Importantly, she experienced no inflammation or infection. Visual evoked potentials measured weeks later improved, indicating stronger signal transmission from her retina to her visual cortex. 

After the procedure, Lucy began reacting to pupillometer and visual examinations when previously they did not disturb her. Because Lucy cannot yet describe precisely what she sees, her increased reaction was itself an important indicator of change. Pupillary responses decreased after a few weeks but remained above pre-injection levels.

Given the success and the limitations of this strategy (among them: sourcing mitochondria from muscle biopsy is not a great long-term solution), we are exploring other ways to isolate and administer Lucy's autologous mitochondria, which we are now isolating from autologous stem cells derived from fibroblasts, a process that takes six or so weeks and requires significant management of the cell culture.

While transplanted mitochondria may improve the function of existing neurons and supporting cells, they are unlikely to result in optic nerve regeneration. Lucy's retinal ganglion cells have already suffered severe atrophy, so even in the best case this strategy has limitations.

In the last two weeks, Lucy's daily visual rehabilitation has begun to produce significant results. She can now reliably track objects both horizontally and vertically when before she could not. At first the objects presented to her had to be illuminated to be seen. More recently, she can track projected images and unilluminated objects.

Lucy is far from having functional vision so we are very open to ideas and potential solutions. 

We welcome ideas posted here on X as well as emails to eye@aoinst.org.

Thank you!
author: BillAckman
quoted_text:
At midnight on February 6th, earlier this year, the doorbell to our apartment rang. The doorbell was followed by a pounding on the door.  I answered the door and a security person in our building handed me his phone. It was my oldest daughter Eloise. She had found my 26-year-old daughter unconscious on the floor of her apartment and had called 911. The EMT team was already there, but they did not know what was wrong with Lucy or to which hospital they would take her.  

I threw on some clothes and jumped in an Uber heading east toward Brooklyn. (Lucy lived alone in Williamsburg.)  On the way, I learned that they were taking her to Elmhurst, a City trauma hospital in Queens.  I arrived about five minutes after the ambulance to join Eloise, Lucy’s mom, and a friend, and waited to learn what was wrong. 

After about 15 minutes, I asked a nurse where she was. I looked over his shoulder to his computer. Next to her name, it said “non-responsive.” I walked into the emergency room and wandered around looking for her until I found her unconscious on a gurney surrounded by several doctors and nurses.  

By about 2:30am with the results from a CAT scan, Lucy’s doctors had determined that she had a massive brain hemorrhage and would need an emergency hemicraniectomy to release the pressure on her brain and remove the blood from the hemorrhage.  I called our wonderful friend and family doctor Eddie Fisher and explained what was going on.  He  woke up Josh Bederson, Chairman of Neurosurgery at Mount Sinai, to find out more about Zach Hickman, the neurosurgeon on call that night. Dr. Bederson said Hickman was an excellent surgeon, which was comforting as we had no choice.

The surgery to save Lucy’s life began around 3:15am and finished around 5:30am. It was successful. 

The following day, I joined Lucy in an ambulance while she was being transferred to Mount Sinai on Madison Avenue. Later that day, we determined from Lucy’s Oura ring that her hemorrhage had occurred around 9am, which meant that more than 19 hours had passed from the time of the hemorrhage to the completion of the surgery to release the pressure on her brain (I only wish @ouraring had an alert for this kind of a medical event. Imagine it could call a family member if the wearer doesn’t cancel the alert). 

I later learned that the standard of care is not to do surgery to save a patient with a large brain bleed if more than five hours have passed since the hemorrhage. Even when the surgery is done, I was told that the likely outcome for the patient is a few months in a nursing home and death from pneumonia.

When I met Lucy’s doctors, I did my best to inspire them: “Let’s see what can be accomplished if we give her the best care possible and we invest unlimited resources to restore her to life.” And I promised that whatever we learned we would make available to everyone. 

Dr. Chris Kellner, her neurosurgeon, and Dr. David Putrino, Director of Rehabilitation Innovation for the Mount Sinai Health System have led Lucy’s care team since that day. Words cannot describe the remarkable and compassionate care that she has received beginning with the EMT team and then from nurses, doctors, therapists, and the army of people who have worked to save her and return her to life. To this day, we have a daily Zoom where we discuss her progress and make adjustments to her care.  While her care and oversight have been incredible, the learnings for the Mount Sinai team have also been elucidating and will assist in the care of many others.

Lucy began in a bad place. She was in a coma for several weeks and then awoke not being able to breathe on her own, unable to walk, see or speak. 

Over the last six months, she has recovered her cognition – she understands everything including her circumstance – is able to walk a hundred or more steps at a time with assistance, is making progress with sounds, vowels and consonants and the beginnings of speech, but she remains unable to see. 

Each day, she makes a little progress, and daily progress compounds.  Every day I tell her that she just needs to make a little progress and it won’t be long before she is back.

We remain optimistic that Lucy will return to normal function. It will likely take years, but I believe it is only a matter of time, hard work, and technological progress, along with some, and perhaps a lot, of divine intervention.  

Many people have been praying for Lucy and we are incredibly grateful for the prayers and remarkable support she has received. Lucy’s friends have been with her every day since the beginning, and their presence and friendship have saved her life and helped to rebuild and maintain her spirit.  And on a very positive note, Lucy’s challenge has brought together our entire modern family who have all been incredibly devoted to her care and recovery.

Lucy's vision and other faculties may require some form of brain computer interface, work that is underway at Neuralink, Precision Neuroscience, Science, Synchron, Nudge, and other companies in the space. 

If you are going to have a devastating brain injury, now is the best time in history for that to happen. We are living in a world when you can be confident that the blind will soon see again.  We are going to do everything we can to help make that happen, including by assisting existing companies in the space.

With respect to our promise to make Lucy’s care available to others, we have made good progress. In May, a real estate colleague made me aware of a 93% vacant, brand new, 400,000 square foot Class A+ purpose-built biotech facility on  West End Avenue between 65th and 66th Streets that missed the market and was available for sale. The Pershing Square Foundation acquired the building 60 days later. 

We also put under contract an adjoining 130,000 square foot building at 320 West 66th Street that is currently being used by Saturday Night Live for studio space. The building has 35-foot ceilings with massive column-free spaces that can be converted into superb rehabilitation facilities.  We will close on the SNL building in December. 

We are also acquiring an adjoining vacant lot with additional air rights.  With just the existing zoning rights, we can add a 150,000 square feet for a total of 680,000 square feet, a lab footprint larger than Rockefeller University, and that’s without including the potential for an upzoning that would allow for substantially more buildable area on the site’s 3.4 acres with spectacular views of the Hudson.

Our goal is to build the world’s greatest brain research, rehabilitation, recovery, human optimization, and longevity institute.  We have named it The Ackman Oxman Institute or the AOI for lack of a better name, but also to reinforce the point that Neri and I and our family are all-in on the mission. 

The AOI will be patient-centric. It will not be an academic research institute that produces lots of papers, a Nobel Prize winner or two, but little if any results for patients. We will be laser-focused on cures, treatments, devices, rehabilitation and exercise equipment, and targeted and basic research with a goal of massively accelerating the time from idea to innovation to production to helping a patient. 

While the AOI will be a non-profit, it will have highly commercial instincts. The AOI will have its own venture funding and will work to develop innovations to create companies that we will seed, assist, and spinout to ensure technologies, treatments, techniques, and drugs get to patients as promptly as possible. 

On one 3.4 acre campus in what is still the greatest city in the world, we will do neurosurgery, neuroscience, rehabilitation, nutrition, BCI and device development, human trials, hyperbaric oxygen treatments, and life extension programs, and we will mandate and incentivize collaboration among the teams with no silos, politics, bureaucracy, or any other constraint that is inconsistent with the mission.  

Mount Sinai will be an important partner and deservedly so, but it won’t be our only hospital or medical school partner as we don’t believe any institution has a monopoly on the best ideas or the best talent.  We don’t believe in exclusive relationships because that is not in the best interest of patients.

Five years ago, we considered launching a brain institute inspired by Neri’s mom who sadly died from Alzheimer’s. We couldn’t make the math work as the real estate was too expensive and we believed it would be too difficult to recruit the best talent from universities to our effort.  

Since then, the real estate became available at a 70% discount, universities became a much less attractive place to work due to politics outweighing meritocracy, protests that disrupt learning, the curse of antisemitism, and a decline in funding. Fortunately, during the same time, I made sufficient personal economic progress to make the AOI possible.  

The advance of AI in the last few years will also enable us to greatly accelerate our mission. AI still has a lot to learn about human intelligence and the brain, and the AOI should be at the forefront of the interplay between the brain and AI.

Today, I am making a public filing disclosing a gift from Neri and me of ~$400 million or 10,000,000 shares of Pershing Square Inc. (PS) to the AOI.  It is very early days for Pershing Square so these shares are intended to anchor the long-term work of the AOI as the shares compound over time while generating what we expect will be a growing stream of quarterly dividends to fund the Institute.  

We will also be announcing an additional gift of similar and potentially greater size which won’t be in the form of Pershing Square stock to provide the AOI with the short- and intermediate-term runway necessary to enable it to achieve its goal of becoming a self-sustaining institute, which reinvests all of its revenues, royalties, and the economic rewards of company formation to advance the fields of brain health and human longevity.  

Neri and I have chosen to anchor the funding of the AOI to maintain vision alignment and limit the need for the organization to focus on fundraising. We expect the AOI to be the best-resourced brain, rehab, recovery, and longevity institute in the world.

We are grateful to have been able to form a board which includes Dean Kamen (our generation’s Thomas Edison), George Yancopoulus (CEO of Regeneron), James Rothman (Nobel Laureate), Bernardo Sabatini (neuroscientist), Chris Kellner (neurosurgeon), Olivia Flatto (CEO Pershing Square Foundation), Neri Oxman, and myself.

We have recently identified a CEO who we expect to announce by October along with other key hires, and are beginning searches for a Chief Scientific Officer, a Chief AI/Technology Officer, a Chief Operating Officer, a Chief Financial Officer, and other key leadership roles.

If you find what we are building compelling and want to be part of the leadership team that creates and builds the AOI from a standing start, please send an email to: search@aoiinst.org with a short note as to why you believe you can help.  Please include your best three ideas for the AOI along with a summary of your background and your most important accomplishments.  

We promise strict confidentiality to those expressing interest in working with us.

We have learned from Lucy that the brain can recover from even catastrophic injury. There is so much more work to be done as the mind is a terrible thing to waste.

For details from my Pershing Square SEC filing see:

https://t.co/gZKafCw6Ia

text:
I found this long post from OpenAIs chief scientist a bit bonkers. Outstanding, but bonkers. 
Outstanding because you see someone smart and honest reason carefully through a very, very hard problem. Bonkers because of what follows from that reasoning. 
1. We do not understand alignment ("I believe that no lab has solved alignment and monitoring to a sufficient degree to continue responsibly scaling at maximum speed for much longer. I expect and hope for voluntary slowdowns to become commonplace until shared safety bars are established.") You want to teach machines how to love? Anyone has any idea of how to teach anyone how to love?
2. We are proceeding by making it up as we go ("The study of deep learning-based AI is largely an experimental science. We put a lot of effort⁠ into building principled algorithms and making testable predictions, but fundamentally, our large-scale training runs are experiments, and we are sometimes surprised by their results. Moreover, as the systems become more capable, the results become harder to interpret.") 
3. It is getting harder to figure out what the machines are doing and thinking ("The AI is becoming better at reasoning about and manipulating its own reasoning process.
With improved pretraining performance, we also see the models become much smarter even without using verbalized reasoning at all.")
4. Hence lets go forward fast into the unknown ("The strongest argument I see for continuing to train much smarter models quickly is the need to build defensive systems against the dangers posed by other AI.")

Uber will be in second place with 35% market share, with two dozen partners putting absurdly cheap Chinese, Japanese, and purpose-built robotaxis into their fleet -- as no car maker wants to go head-to-head with Tesla building cars AND building a network. 

Waymo will buy a car maker in the next 12 months, creating a hybrid of Tesla and Uber: full-stack cars built in its factory, deployed on its network, and also added to Grab, Lyft, Uber, and other networks to increase utilization.  

The big story?

Someone will need to fund FIVE TRILLION DOLLARS WORTH OF CARS 

120M+ cars @ $40,000 each on average; some will be 15-20k two-seaters, some will be premium SUVS at $80,000. 

$7-10T+ in annual revenue is at stake for AVs alone. 

At a 20-40%+ gross margin, $1-2T+ in EBIDA/cash flow, we will be talking about ~20-30T in market cap. 

Waymo and Uber are worth ~$120B and $150B; Tesla is worth $1.4T at the moment. 

There's 18-28T in market cap about to be created. 

Please run this through your own LLMs and models... move the variables around however you like. $5 average ride, $10 average ride, $50k average vehicle cost, etc. 

10% of total rides... 50% of total rides... 

... however you slice it, this will be the largest market in the world for AI over the next decade. 

After that, human robotics will be the TAM/biggest market cap opportunity in the world... but we can do that model next.

text:
GPT 6 Astra is estimated to have ~1.2T Active Parameters and ~10T Total Parameters.

Reports indicate pre-training for GPT-5.5 (codename Spud) concluded on March 24 at the Abilene campus. Astra's pretraining run (Doug) would have taken over that cluster after that, OpenAI confirmed the math results were achieved by an internal version of Astra on August 1. So pretraining ran roughly late March to late June/early July, that is ~90–110 days.

Abilene's operational figure was approximately 150,000 to 200,000 GPUs as of May 2026, with inference sharing the site. So ">100k" for the run means 100 to 150k GPUs.

Around August 25, information circulated that OpenAI had completed a base model called "Bel" with over 10 trillion parameters, successor to Doug. Bel finished ~Aug 25 but Astra was already doing math Aug 1, so Astra is almost certainly on Doug, and Bel is a later model.

Compute for pretraining alone: 120k GPUs × 2.25e15 (BF16) × 0.30 MFU × 100 days ≈ 7e26 FLOP. Range 4e26 to 1.5e27 depending on FP8 and MFU.

Whole 100 days on pretraining, which is now plausible since RL ran afterward (the big RL run was restarted in August per Vellum/CNBC reporting).

Now the data wall does real work. Solve N_active = C / (6·D):
Tokens D          N_active at 7e26
40T                    2.9T
60T                    1.9T
80T                    1.5T
100T                  1.2T

Realistic 2026 corpora with synthetic data and repeats top out ~60–100T, so active params land at 1 to 2T. Even at the conservative 4e26 end with 80T tokens, you get ~830B active.

Astra bills $50/M output at 62 t/s vs Sol's $30/M, a 1.7x price step, consistent with roughly 1.5 to 2.5x active params over its predecessor, not a 10x jump. Rough, but it argues against the >2T end.

Active parameters: ~1T–1.5T (central ~1.2T)
Total parameters: ~10–14T assuming 8–12x MoE sparsity (GPT-4's leaked ratio was ~6.5x; modern large MoE runs 10x+)

text:
从下面两张图片里你能发现什么？

没错

这是我这一阵在Robinhood Chain扫链的过程中发现的两个畜生Dev团队流水线式发盘手法

你只要冲的频率足够高，就一定有买到过它们发的盘子

看完这条推文以后再看到这个公式化打法，跑

严格来说不是不能P，是不能钻

我给大家总结一下，买过的当复盘，没买的当预防

1.先说图1的手法

这个团队发的盘子非常的多，而且频率非常高

但给浇过几次就知道了，他们大致就图里的3个步骤

（1）会先发布一条长文预热
（2）把CA的Robinhood Chain区块浏览器链接直接发出来，如图1中间的部分，偶尔会是一个销毁的说明，但依旧链接
（3）宣布上线+玩法概述，这一条会被它们的X置顶，最重要的是，格式不变，三段式：XXX上线啦+CA+它们这个畜生壳子改变了什么

这三件事，别的项目也会做，但这个团队格式都不改，就这样发了一轮又一轮

最重要的是，据我观察，这三个步骤他们会在4-6小时内做完

所以我现在扫链，看到熟悉的置顶风格，再往下验证另外另外两个东西，依旧公式化出现，直接关闭

_____________________________________

2.图2的手法

这个发盘频率没有前一个多，但是更难防

（1）他们的项目通常会发两个演示视频，一个网页端一个移动端

这两个视频看完，谁不迷糊？

我们会以为这个项目做出来了产品，并推出了一个验证产品概念的APP

一般人到这里，就信了八成了

你不自己去验证会真以为自己买到好东西了

我是买过一个他们的盘子后，在被套的状态下才去验证了产品，其实就是个非常拉胯的静态页面

这个时候我还只是种下了怀疑的种子

（2）直到我偶然间复制了它们其中一条推文在X上搜了一下，好家伙好几个同样文案的项目

再进一步深挖

（3）发现这个畜生团队，连移动端演示时的手机都没换

我对比了三四个它们的项目，发现还真是🤡

根据另外一个不知名“侦探”先生的深挖，这是一个希腊团队

所以这个流水线的筛选，就看两个：视频演示的手机+网页和移动端套模板演示

最抓马的是他们的网页端演示通常在1分钟出头，通常在1分06-1分09秒

_____________________________________

这两个项目包装起来，各种概念很容易让你以为它是个真家伙

简直就是“穿西装打领带，生意就是割韭菜”

他们发出来的盘子，经常只有一波，少数有两波了，然后就换下一个继续割了

说到这里，上面这两个只是一众畜生发盘的手法之二

正所谓道高一尺魔高一丈，难免他们又会再改，那以后扫链怎么办呢？

我的解决办法就是：
（1）先加收藏观察，吃不到一段就不吃，好东西是有二段甚至三段的机会的(RB上多的是真归零和假归零)
（2）如图3，让AI(ChatGPT的工作模式)帮你验证他们的产品是否已经正式部署

这两步要一起做的，因为不是初步上线没正式部署的就不行

而是我们在一边观察它行情的走向的时候，去跟踪验证它产品的进展

这也是我这几天实践下来，胜率相对高的一个简单方法

因为第一波上线，大家冲的可能是这个项目的概念

这第一波就告诉了我们它这个概念被市场的资金短暂认可，后面就需要求证了(实测)

也就是重复我上面那两步

最后结论：帮你们避坑=帮你们省钱=帮你们赚钱

text:
ICOs are getting a new breath of life, and this time hopefully with a better design.

In 2017 they democratized access to the public, but as with any nascent market most were outright scams that had bad incentives and regulatory clampdown. This time around, what’s changed isn’t the idea of public token raises, but the mechanics of capital formation: ultimately solving for who gets access (those with skin in the game + alignment), how allocations are decided (what do you bring to the table), and how communities are embedded from day one into the project that is raising.

There is an ongoing cry for more transparent raises, one that allows the public/ retail to enjoy the upside as well and not just price discovery happening in private markets. The entire market is tired of extreme high valuation launches and insider allocations → reflecting a shift away from low-float/high-FDV private rounds that leave retail holding the bag and becoming EL for most of the time.

A recap on ICOs
An ICO (Initial Coin Offering) is basically a public sale where a project offers tokens (in exchange for ETH/stablecoins) directly to users to bootstrap both capital and community.

The principal behind it is to push ownership toward users and builders rather than just private funds or the team. Prioritize broad distribution (you want as many people championing for your protocol), contribution-based ownership (merit-based based on capabilities), and micro-communities (cults) as the engine of durable networks. Study all the ICOs that have succeeded till today: $ETH, $SOL, $BNB and $LINK are some good examples.

Problem with current raises 
• High FDV launches with a tight float: this invites unlock overhangs and misaligned holders
• Lack of price discovery: this happens in private markets with follow-up rounds and OTCs on secondaries; when projects finally TGE, its a straight down only for price
• Exit liquidity: retails are often used as exit liquidity, due to the point mentioned above 
• FCFS sale benefits selected few: bots are usually the fastest with code and scripts, leaving majority priced out 
• Airdrop mercenaries: industrial operations to farm points campaigns

How the new gen of launch platforms is solving
• Reputation-weighted access: who you are and what you contribute > FCFS
• Creator/staker pools: skin-in-the-game before TGE
• Data-driven discovery and scoring: to prioritize aligned holders
• Compliance-by-design: MiCA-aligned, clear KYC/geo rules) to widen the funnel responsibly (ensure “checks and balances”

Diving into 5 different launchpads at play
a) @HoloworldAI (HoloLaunch)
• An AI-native launchpad that pairs token sales with a creator flywheel (Ava/Agent tools)
• Beyond public pools, staker and creator pools route allocations toward users who actively produce and distribute project-aligned content → turning marketing into a participatory asset
• However, HoloWorld has to fight memecoin giants like https://t.co/sX4bYJBF2D that already dominate Solana attention, forcing Holoworld to subsidise creator inflows to stay relevant

b) @buidlpad (Binance)
• Offers curated, KYC-compliant public sales run by an ex-@Binance Launchpad operator
• Heavy emphasis on strict selection for participants → the curation “pays for itself” via better holder quality and cleaner post-TGE behavior (chart wise)
• Projects launched on Buidlpad so far include @solayer_labs, @saharaai, @Lombard_Finance, @FalconStable and @MMTFinance
• Seems there is a 100% Binance listing streak for the projects launched on Buidlpad, however it also represents a single-point-of-failure, since a future delisting or stricter CEX policies (which end up not listing) would break their USP

c) @legiondotcc (Kraken)
• MiCA-first, reputation-based public fundraising with a @krakenfx partnership 
• A composite Legion Score (on-chain activity, GitHub repos, social credibility) gates allocations and reduces sybil and bot farming allocations
• The goal is aligning cap tables with value-add participants and is important in the era of compliant, reputation-weighted public sales
• On-chain wash trading or paid social engagement can inflate Legion Scores, breaking its “merit over money” USP 
• The recent oversubscribed sale (@yieldbasis) saw sale demand 100x the original target; constant refund cycles frustrate even high-score users and raise transparency concerns

d) @echodotxyz (Coinbase)
• A capital-formation and discovery layer integrated with @Coinbase (recent acquisition for $375m is good for larger distribution; potential integrations with Coinbase accounts and Wallet)
• The pitch is simple: institutional grade, compliance, distribution, and on-chain transparency
• Offers democratised access: Any qualified individual can invest alongside T1 VCs without creating legal entities or wiring fiat across borders
• Access however still requires KYC and (for some deals) accreditation; complete open retail participation is still not guaranteed
• Coinbase acquisition will mean that in the future, every Echo raise would be scrutinised as an unregistered securities offering (due to Coinbase’s US affiliations)

e) @KaitoAI (Capital Launchpad)
• A social-graph + on-chain relevance platform (AI-driven merit system limits whales & bots)
• Since Kaito was known for its social graph (Yaps), there is a seamless tie-in with Yaps leaderboards which gives active researchers (can be argued that many are bots farming engagement) priority, recycling social data back into deal flow
• Projects set terms; users pledge; teams assign Preferred allocations based on reputation/alignment
• Four of the last six tokens (e.g., Novastro -69 %, Everlyn -53 %) now sit below IDO price, could erode confidence for future sales
• The Yaps algorithms remain vulnerable to spam and engagement farming and low-value content can still climb to top tiers of individual leaderboards, skewing token allocations
• Opaque Scoring: because the Yap algorithm is not public; small accounts complain of “yaps jail” and there is no transparency in terms of allocation

What still holds true after all these years post the first wave of ICO in 2017: distribution builds community (cult-like followers who will be your evangelists); communities demand value (we are all here to speculate and create gen wealth); and value attracts builders and capital (attract developers to build things for users, and people will fund interesting and exciting projects).

ICOs in 2017 proved that open distribution can bootstrap networks, the current launch mechanisms will test whether reputation gating, creator/staker pools, and CEX distributions can make public raises credible again.

text:
Often times in your career and life, you will come across a point where you are making a choice between two equally great decisions

These are the ones where there is no black or white right choice. You know that regardless of whichever you pick, the regret of not picking the other will cloud over your shoulder for the rest of your life

There is a lot of advice out there on how to deal with these situations, including just tossing a coin and making a judgement call while the coin hangs in the air

Jeff Bezos famously coined the phrase “regret minimization” where you go down the path that would result in the least amount of regret

In my opinion, the best approach is to actually work backwards and imagine what you would want in your obituary. Then make the choice that best aligns with that note

Working backwards from your death is often far more clarifying than looking forward

An agent researching activity on Robinhood Chain could pull transfers, swaps, and other onchain data to understand what is actually happening.

Most of this infrastructure is still aimed at devs and companies, but the direction is becoming pretty clear.

@RobinhoodCrypto is pushing deeper into agentic trading and payments, while projects around it are building the accounts, data, and transaction rails agents need to operate.

The next question is whether that narrative can attract real liquidity and users.

text:
There’s a ton of “if you had invested $1,000 in <successful stock> 25 years ago, you’d have x today!”, but sometimes it’s interesting to look at the rest of them.

What if you had invested in one of the most exciting growth names a century ago?

In 1926, the major market themes were aviation, office/industrial automation and electrification. One of the best performing big board stocks over the next 3 years was Burroughs Adding Machines - a company that made, you guessed it, adding machines. 

It rode the proliferation of office work to a +1,996% gain over the next 168 weeks. 

And it still survives today. It acquired Sperry Rand in 1986 and the combined company was renamed Unisys, which trades today as UIS. 

If you had invested $1,000 in Burroughs Adding Machines in 1926, the shares would have been worth ~$20,900 at the 1929 peak. And $2,800 today. 

But Burroughs, like many companies a century ago, was an aggressive dividend payer. Assuming you reinvested dividends, you’d have around $35,000 today. 

Seems decent, you outperformed the consumer price index by about 85%. But you’ve underperformed the index by a factor of 640 to 1. 

That same $1,000 invested in the S&P500 (or similar large cap U.S. index, using Shiller/BLS data) would be worth $22.4 million today. 

An investor in 1926 picks a defining technology winner of their generation, a company that manages to continue to exist for a century. But a century was long enough to go through disruption -> hypergrowth -> dominance -> maturity -> tech transition -> renewed relevance -> consolidation -> new disruption -> terminal decline. 

I don’t know exactly what the point is here but I find it pretty interesting considering most of the historical stock selection focuses on companies that survived and thrived.

The crypto x ai bears are missing the whole point. 

The bull case for x402:
- digital goods (i.e., data) and services (i.e., SaaS) are often gated behind paywalls or at least a sign up 
- this adds friction to an agent using these as it goes after a goal
- x402 makes everything permissionless and agent-discoverable. agents only need to buy what they’re using.  
- as agents start to easily discover x402 services, SaaS providers will be incentivized to add their services behind payment gateways to tap into agent distribution
- this becomes a massive flywheel — a true permissionless network of everything in the digital world (and eventually will tap into meat space with robotics and meat proxies)
- if we do this right it can create an autopilot agent economy that gives us more abundance than we could even imagine

Permissionless commercialization + micropayments need crypto.

text:
Crypto moves fast.

New chains launch. New apps break out. Narratives rotate. Attention moves somewhere new every week.

But the things that last tend to have something deeper holding them together.

Solana has developed a nucleus.

A dense core of builders, users, capital, apps, social graphs, ideas, attention and culture that continuously feed into each other.

That nucleus is what makes this feel bigger than any single product, cycle or narrative.

People come and go. Apps rise and fall. The energy gets absorbed, recombined and pushed into whatever comes next.

That’s why culture matters.

The goal was never to own the conversation for a week. It’s to build a global financial layer that lasts for decades.

Technology gives it infrastructure.

Culture gives it gravity.

Solana

author: GavinNewsom

text:
Inspired by a conversation with a friend considering leaving:

There are either three paths:

1. You’re on the right path. 
2. You’re exploring something that *could* be the right path.
3. You’re on the wrong path.

The best way to get on the right path is to leave the wrong path. 

Which looks to other people like not being on a path.

It invites a lot of judgment, questioning — why haven’t you found your path yet?

Whereas being on any path feels safer to others. No one questions it, not to your face anyway. 

Even though you know it’s not the right path. And thus, even though it looks like you’re on the right path, you’re the furthest thing from it, and you’d be closer to the path if you were on no path, even if that feels like a setback because it’s going from certainty to uncertainty. It’s actually a step forward because you’re creating space to find the right path.

A lot of people try to turn the wrong path into the right path. But It’s so much easier to find something great then turn something from bad to great, or even OK to great. 

For those uncertain about whether a path that feels mixed can turn into the right path. Ian Rogers has a good line in the Dialectic podcast: “if the cat is bigger than the shit, keep the cat. If the shit is bigger than the cat, get rid of the cat”.

If you need someone to change behavior — in jobs and in relationships — it’s likely a recipe for unhappiness, since it’s out of your control. Especially if they don’t want to change the way you want them to.  

(Of course, if you’re a reoccurring reason why your paths continuously feel wrong, you’ll need to work on those because you’ll carry your patterns on your next path.)

When I asked you if you would still be on this path in a few years, you definitively said no. OK, so now you’re definitely leaving, it’s now just a matter of when. Why not leave sooner? What’s keeping you? Often the fear of judgment, fear of change, fear of not the unknown, fear of letting someone down (which is inevitable either way), fear of picking something or someone and it not being the thing, 

Well, yes, you might pick the wrong path again, but you’re also on the wrong path now, so what do you have to lose? It might take picking the wrong path a few times before finding the right one.

People rarely regret leaving the wrong path too early, just like people rarely regret firing someone too early. If you have a long string of very short paths, that’s one thing, but usually people feel when they leave something that they could have left it a while ago. 

If anything, more people regret not trying more paths, taking the time to explore and learn more about themselves in the process. People spend way more time in the wrong path (which invites learning of its own kind, to be sure) than they do in the wilderness, exploring things and people that could be the right path.

There are all kinds of illusions and delusions that trick us into seeing the wrong path as the right path — our comfort with any path vs no path, other people’s comfort with us on any path vs no path, the “what if x y z can change”, the “what if no other path is better than this path,” the “what if it’s actually me that’s allergic to paths and therefore I’m the problem and I’ll always be the problem so I might as well just stay here…”

Being in truth with yourself about what you feel and what you want is the only practice that can help you and navigate and discern what path you’re on, and then summon the courage to leave it in order to find the right path for you.

'We want there to be a large focus of the community being a part of our success. . .our goal is to conduct the TGE in a great way, a way that's aligned with our community, a way that optimises for long-term growth of the protocol and healthy growth of the protocol and the token."

'It's our goal to launch the token early. . .launching it not years and years down the line when we're at a five or ten billion FDV, but rather on the slightly earlier side, so they can grow with us and provide feedback.'

'I'd rather us and our investors and others own a smaller piece of a bigger pie that's well aligned, rather than owning 90% of a token and dumping after a pump on the heads of retail. That's not the goal here.'

'Our points holders and really just our users in general feel like stakeholders, which is what we want.'

-------------------------------------------------------

2. olp, variational's in house mm prevents leakage of capital going to external mm, which in turn can be redistributed back to users and fuel the success of the platform:

'Our overall vision is to keep that revenue source within the platform rather than leaking it out to the market makers and then having them kick a small amount back through PFOF. We want to monetise it within one platform and be able to share some of that with the users'

'It's external market makers, the Jumps and the Selinis and what have you of the world. And by the way, this is kind of extractive. The revenue they generate, which is huge, is leaving the Hyperliquid ecosystem. This, by the way, is part of the revenue that eventually becomes our revenue, and we keep it within the ecosystem to benefit the community and lower spreads, and in the future maybe drive economics of the platform.'

'One good thing about OLP being the only liquidity provider on platform is that we could just get back to the basics. It's just user versus OLP providing liquidity. There's no weird HFT games like hiring FPGA engineers. None of that. Getting away from all that is where the cost savings are coming from.'

-------------------------------------------------------

3. the team has studied what has/hasn't worked with other projects

'We've studied other projects very closely - mistakes that I think they've made. I won't say anything negative about them, but I'll say it's a learning opportunity for us, now having full information. . .we learned a lot from Hyperliquid.'

-------------------------------------------------------

4. the team regularly interact with community in various public/private forums and value their input

'We read the Discord every day. Every single day. And I think that's where we get some of our best user feedback, our best listing requests, and our best pulse from the community. . .so many of the best ideas, listing requests, etc. come directly from our community.'

'If you stay in tune with the user base and understand what people want, that's always going to drive home what you can make and turn into something great.'

-------------------------------------------------------

5. the team have publicly stated they want to create the best venue for execution, particularly on rwas

'We're not trying to be the venue for price discovery. We're trying to be the venue for best execution. . .I want to build a platform that gives retail the best possible execution experience and the best possible price.'

'I want people to have the same feeling that I feel in TradFi, which is I don't feel a need to look at the book if I'm trading Tesla or Nvidia, because it's so deep. And I want that liquidity to be on chain.'

'Users are basically going to be forced to trade on Variational because we're going to deliver the best price, the best execution, bounded funding rates on any asset you can imagine.'

-------------------------------------------------------

6. they've also ensured that any investors are here for the long term and aligned with the team's vision

'One of the questions was, can we build this in the long term? Or is this something they have a shorter time horizon on and they're looking to make a quick buck and then exit? Everyone who's on the current cap table is very much aligned with that vision.'

'The vast majority of them are publicly listed. I think they're reputable investors and well known in the space. Token dynamics is something I personally chatted about with most of them, and many of them are supportive of our position to provide a large majority of this alignment to our community, to our users, rather than keeping it in some secret cabal.'

'All of this [being selective re: investors] was done to protect against token dilution, and ensure new names brought onto the cap table have direct ways to contribute to Variational’s long-term growth (with a specific focus on Pro).'

-------------------------------------------------------

7. the tge is merely the beginning of a multi year plan

'It just starts with a TGE, but there are years of building after that. There are years of growing. . .this is just a stepping stone on our way to keep growing for the next many years.'

'I expect that at the time when we TGE, the product vision is not anywhere near completed. We'll still have hundreds of listings remaining, in my expectation. We'll still have Pro on the horizon. We'll still have many other things we're building for our grander vision.'

'We want this to be a five year, 10 year, 15 year project for ourselves. And we're in it for the long run. We're not just going to launch the token and that's the end and give it off to the community. We're going to be there building, competing and making the best product we can.'

8. variational has a foundational culture of rewarding users (over $8m in rewards claimed by users so far)

'Once we took out loss refunds, we realized we had a lot of extra capital on the platform to give back rewards to users. And we want to figure out a way to do that. One of the things we're exploring now is spread rebates, but we're also exploring other mechanisms to give more value back to users.'

'We want to be the most profitable place and most rewarding place for folks to trade. To date we've mostly done that by giving better execution to users, but we also want to see what other incentives we can cook up.'

-------------------------------------------------------

9. the team deliberately delayed the launch of the api to ensure real, early retail users can accumulate points (nb: no points are going to mm)

'One *massively* underappreciated fact about Variational:

We haven’t released a trading API yet. That means trades are manual "click trades" from real humans. No bot farms diluting the pool. Future tokens are going straight to actual users, which is surprisingly rare in this industry.'

'We believe turning it on [the API] would have a huge impact on trading volumes as it would allow for more systematic/advanced trading (and thus increased revenues). But we want to make sure retail users have a solid opportunity to earn points now.'

'What we're really excited for in the coming weeks when we launch our trading API is how the more institutional or informed players can actually plug into our trading API and perform these arbitrages more systematically.'

'If you blow up and get liquidated, or god forbid in the future if there's ever an issue with OLP and it blows up, the capital, that original margin in these smart contracts, stays completely isolated. 'The amount of gas, good lord, that we spend on Arbitrum to move all these funds around real time and keep everyone's balances isolated and safe is very, very difficult, and it would have been a lot easier to do it in one. But it keeps our users safe and it keeps everything transparent.'

'We have third party audits ongoing pretty much at all times. text:
There’s a ton of “if you had invested $1,000 in <successful stock> 25 years ago, you’d have x today!”, but sometimes it’s interesting to look at the rest of them.

What if you had invested in one of the most exciting growth names a century ago?

In 1926, the major market themes were aviation, office/industrial automation and electrification. One of the best performing big board stocks over the next 3 years was Burroughs Adding Machines - a company that made, you guessed it, adding machines. 

It rode the proliferation of office work to a +1,996% gain over the next 168 weeks. 

And it still survives today. It acquired Sperry Rand in 1986 and the combined company was renamed Unisys, which trades today as UIS. 

If you had invested $1,000 in Burroughs Adding Machines in 1926, the shares would have been worth ~$20,900 at the 1929 peak. And $2,800 today. 

But Burroughs, like many companies a century ago, was an aggressive dividend payer. Assuming you reinvested dividends, you’d have around $35,000 today. 

Seems decent, you outperformed the consumer price index by about 85%. But you’ve underperformed the index by a factor of 640 to 1. 

That same $1,000 invested in the S&P500 (or similar large cap U.S. index, using Shiller/BLS data) would be worth $22.4 million today. 

An investor in 1926 picks a defining technology winner of their generation, a company that manages to continue to exist for a century. But a century was long enough to go through disruption -> hypergrowth -> dominance -> maturity -> tech transition -> renewed relevance -> consolidation -> new disruption -> terminal decline. 

I don’t know exactly what the point is here but I find it pretty interesting considering most of the historical stock selection focuses on companies that survived and thrived.

text:
How I do code reviews these days: more code = more selective human review i.e. don't read all the code.

1. Every PR gets a multi-agent first pass. It should find bugs, verify them, rank by severity, suggest fixes. Approval stays a human call on anything that matters.

2. Low blast radius changes on less sensitive code (there's often a lot!) can skip a deep human review once that review is clean. This helps keep the explosion of PRs manageable.

3. Core / sensitive paths still need an owner and human sign-off. That's where you spend time: verification, constraints and earning trust in what the agents can safely cover. You want to keep recoverability.

Agents do the first pass and humans cover blast radius.

Great question from @GergelyOrosz!

this is categorically wrong and i am seeing a lot of similar misunderstandings so i will try my hand at clearing the air

AI/NVDA having deep liquidity has nothing to do with the success of SHROOM, these launchpads like LONG and PONS only continue to create even more liquidity fragmentation which is exactly where SHROOM thrives, i.e. SHROOM will grow more routes to monetize and compound on as more launches happen on LONG, etc.

it's like saying that one really big parking garage makes roads irrelevant

the base case for SHROOM is that it continues to grow as the market maker across tokenized equities, compounding fees (1) back into LP depth and (2) into SHROOM buybacks, targeting volatility (monetizing arb opportunities) + cross-asset flows (including inserting themselves into fomo paths which they are actively prioritizing)... you are longing tokenized equities flows vs. just TVL growth in one specific pair (AI/NVDA)

the real bull cases comes into play when you consider things like the longtail of stock tokens outside of the top ~10 that are underserviced (20% slippage on a $1,000 trade) which SHROOM will continue to expand and compound into, with the moonshot kicker being true adoption of direct cross-equity flows

anyways this continues to be one of the more interesting defi experiments of this cycle and i'm keen to see how tokenized equities further evolve through this meta

text:
FOMO 的势头，确实有点猛。

1/ 交易合约两线开花
过去一周，FOMO 产生了 1067 万美元费用，在 DefiLlama Trading Apps 板块排名第一。
排名第二的 Axiom，同期费用为 660 万美元。

FOMO 的永续合约业务也在快速起量。
过去 24 小时，FOMO Perps 交易量达到 5750 万美元，在 DefiLlama Interface Protocols 板块排名第三，仅落后于 tradeXYZ 等头部项目。
关键在于，FOMO 的永续合约功能直到今年 6 月才正式上线。

FOMO 已经证明了：它不仅有用户和流量，还能把这些用户和流量，快速迁移到新的交易场景和金融产品中。
未来如果 FOMO 继续扩展到预测市场、结构化产品等方向，也并不令人意外。

2/ 压力给到了 Axiom 和 GMGN
面对 FOMO 这样的后起之秀，Axiom 和 GMGN 短期内最直接的应对方式，大概率只有两种。

第一，功能跟进。
也就是借鉴并上线类似服务，尽可能缩小产品矩阵上的差距。

第二，发行代币。
通过空投预期、积分体系和激励机制，增强用户黏性，减缓资金与用户向竞争对手迁移。

不过，对 Axiom 和 GMGN 这类已经具备强现金流的产品来说，发币并不是生存所必需的融资手段。相反，代币更像是一张战略牌。
打得好，可以迅速放大增长；打得不好，也可能稀释原本健康的商业模式，并把平台带入更高成本的激励竞争。

long FOMO - https://t.co/WN2bCgxeck
author: iamyourchaos
quoted_text:
重磅：Delphi Digital 将 @fomo_family 列为 2026 年最看好的消费级应用之一
对标千亿美元巨头 Robinhood？

刚深入研读了 Delphi 的 fomo 研报，核心观点很明确：
fomo 有可能成为新一代的“入口级”投机基建，就像当年 Robinhood 把千禧一代带入美股一样。

fomo 传送：https://t.co/WN2bCgwGmM

但这里有个关键问题——fomo 真的能跑出来吗？

1/ 短期竞争格局：fomo vs Moonshot vs https://t.co/FIDev9wgNH
数据层面，战况已经很明显。
▌Moonshot：历史峰值更高，但趋势持续向下，11 月手续费首次被 fomo 超越
▌https://t.co/FIDev9wgNH：依然是体量老大，但核心还是 meme 币发射交易，业务扩张主要依赖收购
▌fomo：收入趋势向上，产品执行力明显更强

产品差异化上，fomo 的路径选择很聪明。
Moonshot 的审批上架机制在快节奏 meme 周期里完全跟不上，fomo 从一开始就走更通用、链抽象路径，避开了纯 meme 赛道的风险。

2/ 长期想象空间：真正的“基础设施”
这是 Delphi 最看重的点。

fomo 的核心优势——移动原生执行 + 社交发现 + 极简 UX——这套组合拳完全可以扩展到远超 meme 币的领域：
RWA
合成资产
杠杆产品
甚至代币化股票

想象一下，如果 fomo 真的能复制 Robinhood 当年的路径：
▌Robinhood：零佣金 + 移动优先，把年轻人带入美股投机
▌fomo：链抽象 + 社交发现，把更广泛的零售用户带入链上投机
关键在于，fomo 如果能突破圈层，触达真正的大众用户。那价值捕获的天花板就完全不一样了。

值得注意的是，Delphi Digital 并非 fomo 的利益相关方，他们没参与此前的融资轮次。
这种第三方看好的分析，可信度显然更高。

text:
$HOOD just landed its first actual underwriter role, the Oura IPO, since winning regulatory approval to underwrite offerings back in June. This is a meaningful step up from what Robinhood was doing before: as a selling-group member, it could only distribute shares other banks had already priced and allocated. As an underwriter, it now sits inside the syndicate itself, involved in pricing, allocation decisions, and issuer-facing work.

Worth noting the timing: Oura, the smart ring maker, has also been stacking its board with public-company veterans from Netflix, Robinhood, and Deliveroo ahead of this listing, standard IPO prep, but it signals the company is taking the process seriously.

The bigger story here is what Tenev has been saying for months: "the question changed from 'why allocate to retail at all?' to 'how big can the allocation be?'" Robinhood turning that retail-access advantage into an actual underwriting seat, rather than just a distribution channel, is the more interesting structural shift, it puts Robinhood closer to the fee economics of IPOs, not just the customer reach.

text:
A meme paired with a 3x short on $PONS is called "TAMPONS"... 

The mechanics for TAMPONS are pretty interesting:

1) Every $TAMPONS trade pays a 1% fee; part of that revenue is continuously routed into collateral backing a 3× short position on $PONS 

2) If PONS falls, the short generates a profit. The system periodically realizes part of it, then uses 75% of the proceeds to market-buy and burn TAMPONS

3) Flywheel: 

TAMPONS volume → fees → larger PONS short → realized profits if PONS falls → TAMPONS buybacks + burns

It isn’t a direct or fully redeemable hedge; holders don’t own the short or have a claim on its collateral. But structurally, TAMPONS converts trading activity & PONS downside into recurring buy pressure for itself

I'd be surprised if @loraclexyz doesn't kingmake this to drive awareness

A memecoin with a treasury permanently betting against the launchpad it lives on is pretty ironic

purely on memetic value alone I'd say hats off to the dev for creating it; for the first time in a while innovation is returning to the trenches and it's a breath of fresh air

I'm seeing several memetic pairing structures with perp positions recently, so I suspect we will see various layers of this infra breakout

Obvious plays to me are:

1) Bidding the infra for pairing of leveraged stock positions like @Perpshood
2) the associated memetic mascots of HYPE / LIT in PURR ($9M) or LIGER ($1M) 
3) Bidding TAMPONS for the pure memetic factor for when PONS pulls back (likely temporarily before it resumes upwards trajectory)

This is insane! People's imagination for using memeFi is hitting new levels

You'll all be familiar with memes pumping real Penny Stonks, but not manipulating in game economies...

$RSTR is attempting to build a MicroStrategy-style treasury, except the reserve asset is Robin Hood hats inside Old School RuneScape

Why now? Because it's on Robonhood chain...

How it works:

1) $RSTR launched on pons against ETH
2) Every trade pays a 1% fee; of which 70% accrue to the token creator + 30% to pons
3) The RSTR operator claims the creator fees, converts the ETH into OSRS gold (assuming through Bond purchases?) uses that gold to buy Robin Hood hats
4) The hats are spread across multiple RuneScape accounts + withheld from sale
5) Removing hats from circulation pushes up the in-game market price, generating screenshots, attention and theoretically more $RSTR trading
6) More $RSTR trading produces more creator fees, funding further hat purchases

I wanted to check this against a third party source to see if this was actually happening... it is!

i) The GE tracker most players use in RuneScape is showing a spike from 700k RSGP to 4.5m now each hat in just two days
ii) The current price you can buy the hats for is > $4.5m RSGP... i checked and max bid to buy more of the supply actually in game (screenshot)

The main challenges to the process is that there's an element that needs to be off-chain with a human intermediary in using the ETH fees to purchase bonds + then in game currency for the RH hats

I'm not a lawyer but as long as they're purchasing the bonds through Jagex then it should be in compliance? Although not sure about intentional manipulation of in game economics?

Even so... if the accounts are banned it permanently removes the hats from the game and hence achieves the same outcome

You can capitalize on this by buying in game before it goes insane or more speculative through their token

Jagex would receive the revenue from Bond sales, but it's not public so we are unable to benefit from that side of the trade

Once again onchain mechanisms being used with memes to draw in more retail attention... this time from millions of RuneScape players!

환헤지는 기존 포지션의 환차손에 대한 헤지
통화 스왑은 국민 연금이 해외 주식을 매입할 때 원화를 달러로 바꿀 때 생기는 달러원 환율 상승을 회피하기 위한 방법

IMF 사이트에서는 통화 당국의 달러 파생상품 포지션(Predetermined   short-term net drains on foreign currency assets (nominal value), Total   forwards and futures in foreign currencies vis-s-vis the domestic currency   (including the forward leg of currency swaps), Inflows, Long positions)을 볼 수 있는데 월별 변화는 다음과 같음

국민연금과의 통화 스왑도 있고 다른 파생 상품도 있지만 전부 국민연금과의 통화 스왑이라고 가정 하고 본 월별 변화

월별 변화 폭이 나름 큰 상태임 

7월 통화스왑잔고가 60억달러 증가했는데 이것은 국민연금이 60억달러 만큼 해외 주식/채권을 매입할 때 한은과 통화 스왑을 맺어 달러를 조달한 것을 의미하며 통화 스왑이 늘어나면 한은은 계약 만기에 달러를 받게 되지만 당장은 달러가 줄어들게 되므로 외환보유액에서는 차감 됨

text:
This is insane! People's imagination for using memeFi is hitting new levels

You'll all be familiar with memes pumping real Penny Stonks, but not manipulating in game economies...

$RSTR is attempting to build a MicroStrategy-style treasury, except the reserve asset is Robin Hood hats inside Old School RuneScape

Why now? Because it's on Robonhood chain...

How it works:

1) $RSTR launched on pons against ETH
2) Every trade pays a 1% fee; of which 70% accrue to the token creator + 30% to pons
3) The RSTR operator claims the creator fees, converts the ETH into OSRS gold (assuming through Bond purchases?) uses that gold to buy Robin Hood hats
4) The hats are spread across multiple RuneScape accounts + withheld from sale
5) Removing hats from circulation pushes up the in-game market price, generating screenshots, attention and theoretically more $RSTR trading
6) More $RSTR trading produces more creator fees, funding further hat purchases

I wanted to check this against a third party source to see if this was actually happening... it is!

i) The GE tracker most players use in RuneScape is showing a spike from 700k RSGP to 4.5m now each hat in just two days
ii) The current price you can buy the hats for is > $4.5m RSGP... i checked and max bid to buy more of the supply actually in game (screenshot)

The main challenges to the process is that there's an element that needs to be off-chain with a human intermediary in using the ETH fees to purchase bonds + then in game currency for the RH hats

I'm not a lawyer but as long as they're purchasing the bonds through Jagex then it should be in compliance? Although not sure about intentional manipulation of in game economics?

Even so... if the accounts are banned it permanently removes the hats from the game and hence achieves the same outcome

You can capitalize on this by buying in game before it goes insane or more speculative through their token

Jagex would receive the revenue from Bond sales, but it's not public so we are unable to benefit from that side of the trade

Once again onchain mechanisms being used with memes to draw in more retail attention... this time from millions of RuneScape players!
