This is a great question, and I think the progression of why I monetize part of my content is worth explaining.

I am an optimist who believes in the good of others, probably to a naive degree.

Back in 2022, after leaving Trillium, I started spending more and more of my time mentoring traders, both online and in person. My hope was that if I helped people become successful, many of them would give back to charity or pay it forward to other traders.

What I learned instead is that most traders don’t give back. Most view PNL and money as their scorecard, and once they earn it, they don’t want to part with it. There is often an “I earned this on my own” mentality.

My naive hopes were pretty badly wrong, and I got burned multiple times. There have absolutely been some very generous exceptions—shoutout to DL @ KTG, NH, AA, and others—but they were exceptions.

So I eventually found myself in a strange position: I was giving away my time and knowledge, helping already-successful traders make even more money, and then hoping afterward that some of that value would make its way toward causes I cared about. Usually, it didn’t.

The same thing happens with free content more broadly. When something is offered for free, people tend to value it accordingly.

A good example is the annual TraderLion conference. It gets 500k+ views, helps thousands upon thousands of traders, and is built around raising money for charity. Yet despite all of that reach and all of the value being provided, it barely raises a few thousand dollars each year.

That experience changed how I thought about this.

I realized I needed to let capitalism do its job. If people receive something they believe has real financial value, they should pay for it. That is why I initially started a Patreon where 100% of the money went to charity.

The course was the more formal extension of that idea. I spent roughly a year building the service I wish I had when I was developing as a trader.

So yes, if you want me to review your trades, answer your specific questions, teach you the details of my edge, or give you access to the highest-value parts of what I’ve learned over my career, you need to pay for it. 

Charging allows me to put a price on something that has value to the person receiving it, and then I can direct that money toward causes I believe in rather than hoping people voluntarily do it afterward (shocker - they don’t).

That is ultimately why I monetize part of my trading education. I started as a naive optimist who assumed that if I gave enough value away, people who benefited would give back. Experience taught me that incentives work much better than hope.

TL;DR: I do charity work and run a nonprofit, but helping traders make more money is not the nonprofit. @Impact_Comp is. If someone receives meaningful value from my trading knowledge, I believe they should pay for it, and monetization gives me the ability to direct that value toward causes I care about.

text:
Man this is so inspiring! 

TL;DR let’s not pretend we’re Sweden, we’re not there yet! But it’s possible to achieve Sweden-level results in El Salvador.

Not overstating it. Humbly working on it, celebrating successes along the way.
author: nayibbukele
quoted_text:
Now, what DO these results tell us?

1. They tell us that 1,198 students in 171 ordinary Salvadoran public schools participating in this program were independently assessed using an internationally comparable instrument.

And their results in reading, mathematics and science were comparable with the average results of students in Germany and Sweden.

That is a fact, supported by an internationally recognized OECD assessment and reported by the World Bank.

2. They tell us that achieving those levels of performance in Salvadoran public schools is POSSIBLE.

This is perhaps the most important finding.

For decades, we have been told that transforming education takes generations.

That poverty determines educational outcomes.

That our public schools simply cannot compete with schools in developed countries.

Yet here we have Salvadoran children, attending Salvadoran public schools, taught by Salvadoran teachers and supported by AI tutors, inside our existing public education system, obtaining results comparable with students in some of the world’s most developed countries.

Does that prove that every Salvadoran student is already performing at that level?

Of course not.

But it proves something enormously important:

There is nothing inherent about being Salvadoran, attending a public school, coming from a lower-income family, or living in a developing country that prevents a child from reaching those levels.

3. It tells us that the conditions associated with these results appear to be replicable.

Imagine that the explanation were that we selected 171 elite private schools, filled them with the country’s wealthiest children, and then announced their scores.

That would tell us almost nothing about whether the model could work nationally.

But that’s not what happened.

These are ordinary public schools.

The advantages associated with participation in the pilot: better tools, connectivity, infrastructure, teacher support, technology and a different educational model, are precisely the things the Government can reproduce.

That doesn’t guarantee the same results when we scale.

But it gives us a very good reason to try.

4. It tells us that expanding the program is worth doing.

A pilot is not supposed to prove that something already works everywhere.

If it did, it wouldn’t be a pilot.

A pilot asks a much simpler question:

“Does this approach show enough promise under real-world conditions that we should expand it and test whether the results can be reproduced at a much larger scale?”

The answer from these results is clearly yes.

The World Bank itself described the results as promising and encouraging evidence ahead of the expansion of the reform.

5. The real test begins NOW.

Going from 171 schools to more than 1,000 schools is much harder.

Going from 1,000 schools to every public school in El Salvador will be harder still.

Scaling introduces new problems.

Some schools have weaker infrastructure.

Some have worse connectivity.

Some teachers will adapt faster than others.

Some communities face greater social and economic challenges.

And implementation quality can decline as a program becomes larger.

All of that is true.

And that is exactly why we are scaling progressively.

The next question is not whether 171 schools can do it.

We now know they can.

The question is whether 1,000 can.

Then whether several thousand can.

And ultimately whether an entire national public education system can.

That is what we intend to find out.

6. And yes, the future national PISA results that will be published in 2029 will matter enormously.

Those will tell us something different.

PISA for Schools tells us what is happening in the schools participating in this reform.
National PISA will tell us what is happening across the country.

Those are different questions, and serious people should not confuse them.

2/2🧵👇🏼

author: nayibbukele
quoted_text:
A few days ago, I shared the World Bank’s summary of the results of the PISA for Schools assessment conducted in 171 Salvadoran public schools participating in our education pilot.

Since then, I have seen some legitimate questions about what these results mean, as well as some claims about what they supposedly don’t mean.

So let’s be very precise.

First, what we NEVER claimed:

1. We never claimed these results represent the national average.

They don’t.

This was not the national PISA assessment. 

It was PISA for Schools, conducted specifically in the 171 public schools participating in our pilot program.

That is precisely why my original post said: 

“These are the results of our pilot program, which includes AI tutors and has been running in 171 public schools for just over a year.”

A pilot is, by definition, not the entire country.

2. We never claimed that these 171 schools were a statistically representative sample of every school in El Salvador.

They weren’t selected randomly from all Salvadoran schools.

They were selected to participate in the pilot because they were schools where the program could initially be implemented more easily: they had certain basic infrastructure and connectivity requirements, and school communities capable and willing to implement a new educational model.

That creates a selection effect, and it should be acknowledged.

But there is an important distinction here.

These schools were NOT selected because their students had exceptional academic results.

They were not our “best schools.” Not even close.

We didn’t search the country for the highest-performing schools or students and then test them.

They are normal Salvadoran public schools, urban and rural, in different parts of the country, serving ordinary Salvadoran families.

And the characteristics that made implementation easier: connectivity, infrastructure, trained teachers and willingness to adopt the program, are also things that can be replicated in other schools.

They are not innate characteristics of the students.

We can install connectivity.

We can improve infrastructure.

We can train teachers.

We can provide the same technology.

We can deploy the same educational tools.

In fact, that is exactly what we are doing.

3. These results also do NOT prove that AI tutors, by themselves, caused the improvement, although we believe they are a MAJOR part of these results.

Our pilot is broader than that.

It includes changes in teaching, support for teachers and principals, educational materials, monitoring and evaluation, technology, and AI tools, among other interventions.

Our AI tutors and learning platforms are being developed with @grok, @Kira_Learning, and support from I Hate Flying Bugs.

And the broader transformation of our education system is being supported by the @WorldBankGroup, @AgendaCAF, and @el_BID.

All of these interventions can also affect student motivation and engagement.

But that distinction matters: if students become more motivated BECAUSE of the program, that is not necessarily a flaw in the program or an explanation that somehow invalidates the results.

It may be one of the ways the program works.

The same applies to teachers.

For example, the implementation of the AI tutors, including the requirement for teachers to log in and out of the system, coincided with teacher attendance in these schools increasing from 76% to 97%.

If the program causes teachers to attend school more consistently, and that in turn helps students learn more, that is not an advantage that disappears when we scale the program.

It is potentially part of the intervention itself.

Of course, to scientifically isolate the causal effect of AI tutors, teacher attendance, student motivation, technology, training, or any other individual component would require a different experimental design.

Now, what DO these results tell us?

1. They tell us that 1,198 students in 171 ordinary Salvadoran public schools… 🧵1/2👇🏼

9 月 6 日，亨特在 WABC 电台被问到是否会参选总统，回了一句：“如果能得到你的支持，我可能不得不参选。”

他目前还没有正式宣布参选，但发币时间紧跟这次表态，很容易被理解为在给个人政治 IP 预热。

text:
The hard part isn't building trading agents. It's knowing which ones to trust. Excited to back @roostooAI in ER S4.

Anyone can launch an AI trading agent now. Almost nobody can tell you which ones are good. Backtests are marketing, and the only honest test is out-of-sample performance in a live, adversarial market. Today the only way to run that test is to hand the agent real money and hope.

@roostooAI  is building the qualification layer in between. Agent Factory turns a strategy into an RL-trained agent without writing code. The Arena runs it against live market data alongside human traders and rival agents, ranked continuously on a leaderboard. Agents earn trust through performance before they earn capital, then graduate to DEXs and vaults.

What convinced us:

- Track record becomes the scarce asset. When agents are free to spin up, the bottleneck moves to credible evaluation. Whoever owns the ranking owns the allocation decision.
- Failure should be cheap. Paper trading is the right place for a strategy to break. Roostoo makes that the default path to live capital instead of the step everyone skips.
- The distribution already exists. Roostoo has run competitions with 300+ partners, from Jane Street, Optiver, IMC and Flow Traders to Imperial, NUS, HKUST and IIT Delhi. A standing pipeline of quant talent already competing inside their environment, and every competition produces labeled performance data.

Agents are getting hands. What they still need is a reason to be trusted with the wallet.

Prove it in the arena first.

text:
I made a mistake in my previous calculation: https://t.co/8obSpur6CU

It actually takes only ~100 years to cool Venus down to an Earth-like temperature if we block all solar radiation from reaching its surface and use the intercepted solar energy to power an economically feasible AI data center in Venus orbit.

That means planetary-scale climate engineering may not be as far beyond our technological horizon as it sounds. The biggest constraints may not be the laws of physics, but the scale of humanity’s economy, along with the amount of energy, infrastructure, and industrial capacity we are able to deploy.

At the current pace of growth in energy demand, we may be able to achieve planet-scale electricity generation within a few thousand years, if not sooner.

If we first blocked most or all of the sunlight reaching Venus, the planet could gradually cool. As the temperature falls, the CO₂ atmosphere would eventually cross into a very different phase regime. Venus currently has an atmosphere dominated by CO₂ at a surface pressure of roughly 90 bar, so once the planet becomes sufficiently cold, a large fraction of its CO₂ could potentially condense into liquid or solid reservoirs rather than remaining in the atmosphere.

At that point, the problem changes fundamentally. We would no longer be dealing with an atmosphere containing an enormous amount of gaseous CO₂. We would have a planet covered with concentrated carbon-dioxide reservoirs that could, in principle, be processed, transported, or stored much more efficiently.

In other words, the first stage could be thought of as planetary cooling, while the second stage becomes planetary carbon management.

Yesterday, Europe officially opened its largest industrial carbon capture and storage facility at Yara’s Sluiskil plant in the Netherlands. The project captures and liquefies up to 800,000 tonnes of CO₂ per year from ammonia production, after which the CO₂ is shipped to Norway and permanently stored 2.6 km beneath the seabed.

Some may argue that this facility produces little value. It may be true on Earth. But it could serve as a real-world testbed for technologies that, in a not-too-distant future, might be adapted for terraforming Venus. The basic industrial logic is similar: capture carbon, concentrate it, transport it, and permanently remove it from the atmosphere.

text:
Samsung Foundry Launches Its Counterattack: "Full Capacity" Before Full Operation Even Begins

Samsung Electronics' foundry division is mounting a major counteroffensive in the global foundry market dominated by Taiwan's TSMC, riding on large orders from US big tech companies such as Tesla and Broadcom. The Taylor foundry fab in Texas, which is set to begin pilot operation as early as the end of this month, has already reached "full capacity" with its planned production volume fully booked, and it has been confirmed that the company is also pushing ahead with the introduction of equipment from domestic suppliers for the second fab, which breaks ground at the end of the year.

The move is seen as a decisive bet to secure mass production capabilities on par with TSMC in the 2nm node, the cutting edge process that will determine leadership in the global foundry market next year, and to capture big tech's demand to move away from TSMC.

According to the semiconductor industry on the 8th, Samsung's Taylor fab in the US has effectively reached full capacity before even starting operation, as 2nm orders keep coming in, including Tesla's next generation AI chip "AI5," Broadcom's next generation communications chip, and an AI chip for smart devices from the UK's Arm. The 2nm yield , which stood at around 60% earlier this year, is reported to have recently reached the 80% range, a level that makes mass production possible, helped by the stabilization of yields on existing advanced nodes such as 4nm and 5nm.

The Taylor fab, which Samsung has built since 2022 with an investment of $37 billion (about 52 trillion won), will go through pilot operation early next month and begin volume production next year. Its initial production capacity is 50,000 wafer inputs per month, close to the level of Taiwan's TSMC (80,000). Samsung previously dispatched process, equipment, and yield personnel to the Taylor fab in June and began equipment installation in July.

With the Taylor fab, the core base of Samsung Foundry, entering full capacity, the earnings of the foundry business, long the "sore spot" of the Device Solutions (DS) division, are also rising quickly. At its recent earnings call, Samsung projected that its 2nm order volume this year would more than double from last year. Nvidia's inference only chip "Groq 3" also entered mass production last month. Built on the 4nm process, Groq 3 is a rack scale system that bundles 256 language processing units (LPUs) and is tasked with expanding the inference performance of the next generation AI platform "Vera Rubin." Samsung's recent price increase of up to 15% on its 4nm foundry services has also contributed to the improvement in earnings.

Preparations for the second Taylor fab, which breaks ground at the end of this year with mass production targeted for 2030, are also accelerating. Samsung is reported to have recently asked major suppliers to obtain safety certification in advance for the chip production equipment to be installed in the second fab. Some suppliers are also said to be pushing plans to dispatch dozens of personnel on site for the construction of the second Taylor fab.

The back and forth battle for leadership is heating up as well. In the US, Intel issued $20 billion in new shares last month and is expanding investment in its 2nm class "18A" process and next generation 1.4nm class "14A." Rapidus, the symbol of Japan's semiconductor revival, also completed its 2nm foundry fab in Hokkaido last month and has entered the pilot wafer input stage.

text:
2026 年伊始，美国区块链上市公司 Coinbase 宣布成立量子咨询委员会，以太坊基金会将量子安全升为战略最高优先级，并组建量子安全团队。而美国 NIST(美国国家标准技术研究所) 也给出了量子安全迁移时间节点，种种迹象表明，区块链行业即将迎来巨大的安全挑战。

时间拉近到 2026 年的 3 月 30 日，由谷歌量子 AI 部门的负责人 Ryan Babbush 与以太坊基金及斯坦福大学等相关研究人员发布的论文，彻底敲响了量子末日的钟声，这篇 《保护椭圆曲线加密货币免受量子漏洞攻击：资源估算与缓解措施》表示，在最新的量子资源估算情况下，使用不到 50 万个量子比特，可在几分钟内完成量子攻击，比此前业界估算缩小了 20 倍。相较于之前，谷歌正式把后量子迁移时间表提前至 2029 年，并公开对全行业发出 “最后” 提示。

我们知道，区块链的核心基石是公钥密码学（Public-key Cryptography），近年来量子计算机的算力呈现指数级发展趋势，使得传统的公钥密码学日益受到威胁，媒体通常会给出十分紧迫的量子威胁日期，似乎量子计算机会瞬间摧毁旧的数字世界，但是事实并非如此。面对量子的潜在挑战，区块链行业也在积极地研发量子安全解决方案——例如，比特币社区新推出 BIP-360（Pay to Merkle Root）抗量子提案；以太坊即将到来的抗量子升级 EIP-8141；以太坊二层网络 Optimism 提出的未来 10 年的抗量子路线图等。较于区块链网络升级的复杂性，开发者社区也在打造更 “简易的” 抗量子基础设施，如为比特币用户开发了 “抗量子” 工具 (YellowPages）等，旨在保证其私钥的量子安全性。

当然，随着能够储存量子比特 (Qubit)的量级增加，量子计算机能破解区块链传统密码学的风险的确也在日益加剧。那么，这种威胁的程度到底如何？Web3 行业正在如何应对？未来还有多远实现抗量子？
